descriptions.name: 1,4-Dioxane
descriptions.description_en: A by-product formed when surfactants are ethoxylated, so it appears as a contaminant rather than a listed ingredient. IARC classifies it Group 2B, possibly carcinogenic, and manufacturers are expected to strip it out.

descriptions.name: 2-Butoxyéthanol
descriptions.description_en: A solvent in window and multi-surface cleaners. It passes readily through the skin and, at high exposure, damages red blood cells, the liver and kidneys. Workplace exposure limits apply in the EU and US.

descriptions.name: 2-chloroethanol
descriptions.description_en: The reaction product of ethylene oxide with chloride, measured together with it under the same EU residue limit. Its own genotoxicity is debated, but its presence indicates treatment with a banned carcinogenic fumigant.

descriptions.name: 4-hexylresorcinol
descriptions.description_en: A synthetic anti-browning agent used mainly on crustaceans to slow discoloration. Current use is narrow and residue-controlled. Health: No major concern is established at authorized residues. Broader or higher exposure would require additional safety evidence.

descriptions.name: acesulfame
descriptions.description_en: An artificial sweetener (E950) roughly 200 times sweeter than sugar, often blended with aspartame. Approved in the EU and US with an acceptable daily intake of 9–15 mg/kg, but it is a marker of ultra-processed formulation.

descriptions.name: acetate de sodium
descriptions.description_en: The sodium salt of acetic acid (E262), used as a preservative and to give salt-and-vinegar flavour. It is well tolerated but contributes sodium to the diet.

descriptions.name: acetylated oxidized starch
descriptions.description_en: A starch subjected to oxidation and acetylation to improve stability, clarity, and texture. Health: It is not classified as carcinogenic. The main issue is its use as a structural ingredient in heavily processed products.

descriptions.name: acide acetique
descriptions.description_en: The acid of vinegar (E260), used to adjust acidity and preserve food. It is one of the oldest and most benign preservatives, and taken with a meal it slightly lowers the blood sugar response.

descriptions.name: acide adipique
descriptions.description_en: An acidity regulator (E355) used in powdered desserts and drink mixes. It is produced industrially and considered safe at the low levels permitted.

descriptions.name: acide alginique
descriptions.description_en: A gelling fibre (E400) extracted from brown seaweed. It is not absorbed and behaves as soluble fibre, though large amounts can reduce mineral absorption.

descriptions.name: acide azelaique
descriptions.description_en: A naturally occurring acid from grains, used for acne and rosacea. It is one of the best tolerated actives available, gentle enough for sensitive skin and considered safe during pregnancy.

descriptions.name: acide borique
descriptions.description_en: Boric acid (E284), a preservative now allowed in the EU for caviar only. It is classified as toxic to reproduction under EU chemical law and accumulates in the body, which is why its use is so tightly limited.

descriptions.name: acide citrique
descriptions.description_en: An acid naturally present in citrus fruit, produced for food use by fermentation. EFSA has identified no safety concern at food levels, making it one of the most benign additives.

descriptions.name: acide fumarique
descriptions.description_en: An acidity regulator (E297) that occurs naturally in plants and in human metabolism. It is considered safe at food levels, though the food-grade version is synthesised industrially.

descriptions.name: acide glutamique
descriptions.description_en: Glutamic acid (E620), the free amino acid behind the savoury "umami" taste. It is used to intensify flavour in industrial foods and signals a product built on additives rather than real ingredients.

descriptions.name: acide glycolique
descriptions.description_en: An alpha-hydroxy acid that exfoliates the skin surface and improves texture. EU rules cap consumer concentrations, and it increases sun sensitivity, so daily sunscreen is necessary while using it.

descriptions.name: acide kojique
descriptions.description_en: A skin-lightening agent produced by fermentation, used to fade dark spots. The SCCS caps it at 1% in cosmetics because of concerns about skin sensitisation and thyroid effects at higher levels.

descriptions.name: acide phosphorique
descriptions.description_en: An acidity regulator (E338) that gives colas their sharp bite. EFSA set a combined phosphate limit of 40 mg/kg in 2019 and warned that some groups already exceed it; high phosphate intake concerns kidney and bone health.

descriptions.name: acide propionique
descriptions.description_en: A mould inhibitor (E280) used mainly in industrial bread. It occurs naturally in some cheeses and is considered safe by EFSA, but its presence signals bread built for long shelf life.

descriptions.name: acide salicylique
descriptions.description_en: A beta-hydroxy acid that exfoliates and unclogs pores, effective against acne. Its concentration is capped in EU cosmetics, and it should not be used on children under three or during pregnancy without medical advice.

descriptions.name: acide sorbique
descriptions.description_en: A mould inhibitor (E200) and one of the gentler preservatives, occurring naturally in rowan berries. It is well tolerated, though it can cause mild skin or digestive reactions in sensitive people.

descriptions.name: Acide tartrique
descriptions.description_en: A natural acid from grapes (E334), used to adjust acidity and in baking powder. It is well tolerated and one of the simplest acidity regulators available.

descriptions.name: acides gras
descriptions.description_en: Fatty acids (E570) used as anti-foaming and glazing agents rather than as a food fat. They are refined industrial derivatives, typical of processed formulations.

descriptions.name: acrylamide
descriptions.description_en: A compound that forms when starchy foods are fried, roasted or baked at high heat. IARC rates it Group 2A, probably carcinogenic, and EFSA confirmed it raises cancer risk across all age groups.

descriptions.name: acrylates
descriptions.description_en: Synthetic polymers that form films in nail products, hair styling and long-wear make-up. Cured polymers are stable, but uncured acrylate monomers in nail products are strong skin sensitisers.

descriptions.name: advantame
descriptions.description_en: An artificial sweetener (E969) derived from aspartame and roughly 37,000 times sweeter than sugar, so it is used in minute amounts. Authorised in the EU and US, but a purely synthetic high-intensity sweetener.

descriptions.name: aflatoxine
descriptions.description_en: A natural mold toxin that forms on poorly stored grains, nuts and spices. Classified IARC Group 1 human carcinogen — the confirmed level. Chronic exposure damages the liver and is a leading cause of liver cancer.

descriptions.name: agar agar
descriptions.description_en: A gelling agent (E406) from red seaweed and a plant-based alternative to gelatine. It is not absorbed and behaves as soluble fibre in the gut.

descriptions.name: alcool ethylique
descriptions.description_en: Ethanol in alcoholic beverages is an IARC Group 1 human carcinogen. It is linked to cancers of the mouth, throat, oesophagus, liver, colon and breast, and no safe intake level has been established.

descriptions.name: alginate d ammonium
descriptions.description_en: A seaweed-derived thickener (E403) used to stabilise texture. It passes through the gut undigested and is considered safe at food levels.

descriptions.name: alginate de propylene glycol
descriptions.description_en: A chemically modified alginate (E405) used to stabilise beer foam and dressings. Unlike plain alginates it is reacted with propylene glycol, making it a synthetic derivative rather than a simple seaweed extract.

descriptions.name: Alkylphénols éthoxylés (APEO)
descriptions.description_en: Surfactants used in detergents and textile processing. They break down into alkylphenols, recognised endocrine disruptors that are highly toxic to aquatic life, and their use is restricted under EU REACH rules.

descriptions.name: allulose
descriptions.description_en: A rare sugar found naturally in figs and raisins that is barely metabolised, so it sweetens with almost no calories or glucose response. Large amounts can cause digestive upset.

descriptions.name: Aluminium (casseroles, papier)
descriptions.description_en: Aluminium cookware and foil release small amounts of metal into food, especially with acidic or salty dishes at high heat. EFSA set a weekly tolerable intake that many diets already approach.

descriptions.name: Aluminium chlorohydrate (déodorants)
descriptions.description_en: The active salt in antiperspirants, which works by physically plugging sweat ducts. Health agencies have not established a link to breast cancer, but it is absorbed in small amounts and adds to total aluminium exposure.

descriptions.name: aluminum chlorohydrate
descriptions.description_en: The active salt in antiperspirants, which plugs sweat ducts to block perspiration. No link to breast cancer has been established, but it is absorbed in small amounts and adds to total aluminium exposure.

descriptions.name: aluminum sulfate
descriptions.description_en: An aluminum-containing processing salt used in limited applications. It contributes to total dietary aluminum exposure. Health: Because aluminum can accumulate, repeated exposure from many sources may push intake above the tolerable weekly level, especially in people with reduced kidney function.

descriptions.name: amande
descriptions.description_en: Almonds, rich in vitamin E, magnesium, fibre and monounsaturated fat. Regular nut consumption is consistently associated with better cardiovascular outcomes.

descriptions.name: amidon
descriptions.description_en: Starch extracted from grains or tubers, used to thicken and bulk out food. It is a refined carbohydrate with a high glycemic response and none of the fibre or nutrients of the original grain.

descriptions.name: amidon acetyle
descriptions.description_en: Acetylated starch (E1420), chemically treated to stay stable through processing. It is a refined carbohydrate with no fibre or micronutrients, used purely for texture.

descriptions.name: amidon de ble
descriptions.description_en: Wheat starch separated from the protein and bran of the grain. It behaves like a fast sugar in the body, with little nutritional value — the whole grain is always the better option.

descriptions.name: amidon modifie
descriptions.description_en: Starch chemically or physically altered (E1404) to thicken and stabilise industrial food. Considered safe by EFSA, but it is a refined carbohydrate with no nutrients and a clear marker of ultra-processing.

descriptions.name: Ammoniac
descriptions.description_en: Ammonia and its compounds, used as acidity regulators and processing aids. They are neutralised in the finished food, but ammonia processing can generate unwanted by-products in some applications.

descriptions.name: ammonium aluminum sulfate
descriptions.description_en: An aluminum-containing industrial salt used for firming or processing in limited foods. Health: Repeated intake contributes to total aluminum exposure, which is limited because the metal can accumulate in the body.

descriptions.name: ammonium carbonates
descriptions.description_en: Industrial raising agents that release carbon dioxide and ammonia during baking. They are commonly used in dry biscuits and crackers. Health: Poorly baked or heavily dosed products may retain an unpleasant ammonia odor and cause irritation, but normal baked use is not considered a major health risk.

descriptions.name: ammonium hydroxide
descriptions.description_en: An ammonia solution used in controlled processing and pH adjustment. Most ammonia is removed, reacted, or present at very low residual levels. Health: High residual concentrations would irritate the eyes, airways, and digestive tract and produce a strong odor.

descriptions.name: ammonium sulfate
descriptions.description_en: An industrial salt used in flour treatment, fermentation, and acidity control. Health: No major specific harm is established at permitted levels. Excessive quantities may irritate the digestive system.

descriptions.name: annatto
descriptions.description_en: A yellow-orange colouring (E160b) extracted from achiote seeds, one of the few plant-based dyes still widely used in industry. Generally well tolerated, though it can trigger allergic reactions in a small number of people.

descriptions.name: anthocyanes
descriptions.description_en: Purple-red pigments (E163) extracted from grape skins, berries or red cabbage. They are plant-derived and carry antioxidant activity, but the food-grade version is a concentrated industrial extract.

descriptions.name: Antimoine
descriptions.description_en: A metal used as a catalyst in PET bottle manufacture, which can leach in trace amounts when bottles are heated or stored a long time. IARC classifies antimony trioxide Group 2B.

descriptions.name: argent
descriptions.description_en: Silver (E174) used as a decorative coating on confectionery. EFSA could not complete its safety re-evaluation because of insufficient data on absorption and nanoparticle content.

descriptions.name: argon
descriptions.description_en: An inert gas used to displace oxygen and slow oxidation in packaged food and beverages. Health: It does not react significantly with food and is not considered a safety concern in authorized packaging use.

descriptions.name: arome artificiel
descriptions.description_en: Entirely synthetic molecules, usually petrochemical-derived, built to imitate natural tastes. Their exact composition is not disclosed on the label, and they are one of the clearest markers of ultra-processed food.

descriptions.name: arome bio
descriptions.description_en: Flavouring made from certified organic raw materials, which limits solvents and synthetic inputs. Still a concentrated industrial extract, but a step above conventional natural flavouring.

descriptions.name: arome naturel
descriptions.description_en: Despite the name, these are extracted and concentrated in industrial processes, often using solvents. The precise composition is a trade secret, and their presence signals a product engineered for taste rather than made from whole ingredients.

descriptions.name: arsenic
descriptions.description_en: A heavy metal contaminant found in water, rice and some seafood. Arsenic and inorganic arsenic compounds are IARC Group 1 human carcinogens, linked to skin, lung and bladder cancer.

descriptions.name: ascorbate de calcium
descriptions.description_en: A vitamin C salt (E302) used to protect food from oxidation. It provides genuine vitamin C activity along with a small amount of calcium.

descriptions.name: ascorbate de sodium
descriptions.description_en: The sodium salt of vitamin C (E301), used as an antioxidant to stop food browning and fats oxidising. It retains vitamin C activity and is among the most benign additives.

descriptions.name: aspartame
descriptions.description_en: An artificial sweetener (E951) in diet drinks and sugar-free products. IARC classified it Group 2B, possibly carcinogenic, in 2023, while WHO's JECFA kept the daily limit at 40 mg/kg. Best not consumed daily.

descriptions.name: atrazine
descriptions.description_en: A herbicide banned in the EU since 2004 but still detected in groundwater decades later. It is widely regarded as an endocrine disruptor affecting hormonal and reproductive function, and remains in use in North America.

descriptions.name: avocat
descriptions.description_en: Avocado and olives, both rich in monounsaturated fat, fibre and vitamin E. Their fat profile supports heart health and helps the body absorb fat-soluble vitamins from other foods.

descriptions.name: avoine
descriptions.description_en: Oats, one of the best sources of beta-glucan, a soluble fibre with a proven effect on cholesterol. They release energy slowly and keep you full far longer than refined cereals.

descriptions.name: azodicarbonamide
descriptions.description_en: A flour treatment agent (E927) used to bleach dough and speed up baking. Banned in the EU and Australia, still permitted in the US. During baking it breaks down into semicarbazide and urethane, both flagged for cancer concerns.

descriptions.name: azorubine
descriptions.description_en: Carmoisine (E122), a synthetic red azo dye. EU law requires a label warning that it may affect activity and attention in children, and it is not authorised in the United States.

descriptions.name: azote
descriptions.description_en: Nitrogen gas (E941) used to displace oxygen in packaging and keep food fresh without preservatives. It is inert, makes up most of the air we breathe, and leaves no residue.

descriptions.name: bacon
descriptions.description_en: Salted, cured and smoked pork. It falls under processed meat, classified IARC Group 1 human carcinogen in 2015: regular intake raises colorectal cancer risk through nitroso-compounds formed during curing.

descriptions.name: bakuchiol
descriptions.description_en: A plant compound from babchi seeds, studied as a gentler alternative to retinol. Early trials suggest comparable effects on fine lines with far less irritation, and it is considered suitable during pregnancy.

descriptions.name: basic methacrylate copolymer
descriptions.description_en: A synthetic polymer used mainly to coat food supplements and control how tablets dissolve. Health: It is poorly absorbed. Safety relies on low residual monomers, controlled purity, and restricted use.

descriptions.name: benzene
descriptions.description_en: An industrial solvent and petroleum by-product. IARC Group 1 human carcinogen with an established causal link to leukaemia. It has no legitimate use in food or cosmetics and appears only as a contaminant.

descriptions.name: benzoate de potassium
descriptions.description_en: A preservative (E212) closely related to sodium benzoate. It can form traces of benzene when a product also contains vitamin C, and may trigger hives or asthma in sensitive people.

descriptions.name: benzyl alcohol
descriptions.description_en: An aromatic alcohol used mainly as a solvent or carrier in flavorings. Food exposure is limited, but it is biologically active at high doses. Health: Large systemic doses can depress the nervous system and disturb metabolism. Newborns are particularly vulnerable to high medicinal exposure, although food amounts are far lower.

descriptions.name: beta-cyclodextrin
descriptions.description_en: A ring-shaped carbohydrate manufactured from starch and used to trap, protect, or carry flavors and other compounds. It has a relatively low acceptable daily intake. Health: High exposure can exceed the recommended daily limit. The restriction is based on systemic effects observed at higher doses, not on a cancer classification.

descriptions.name: beurre
descriptions.description_en: Butter, made by churning cream with nothing added. High in saturated fat, so moderation applies, but it is a natural fat that needs no industrial processing.

descriptions.name: beurre de cacao
descriptions.description_en: The natural fat pressed from cocoa beans. It is stable, does not require hydrogenation, and is what distinguishes real chocolate from products made with vegetable fat.

descriptions.name: bha
descriptions.description_en: Butylated hydroxyanisole (E320), a synthetic antioxidant in fats, snacks and cosmetics. Classified IARC Group 2B, possibly carcinogenic to humans, and flagged by EFSA as a suspected endocrine disruptor.

descriptions.name: bht
descriptions.description_en: Butylated hydroxytoluene (E321), a synthetic antioxidant in fats, cereals and cosmetics. EFSA re-evaluated it as safe within a low daily limit; IARC does not classify it as carcinogenic.

descriptions.name: bicarbonate
descriptions.description_en: Baking soda, a single-ingredient raising agent that has been used for generations. It is simple, effective and free of the aluminium found in some baking powders.

descriptions.name: bisulfite de calcium
descriptions.description_en: A sulfite preservative and firming agent (E227). It carries the same allergen labelling requirement as other sulfites and can provoke asthma symptoms in sensitive individuals.

descriptions.name: bisulfite de potassium
descriptions.description_en: A sulfite preservative (E228) used in wine and processed fruit. Like the whole sulfite family, it must be declared above 10 mg/kg and can trigger reactions in sulfite-sensitive people.

descriptions.name: bisulfite de sodium
descriptions.description_en: A sulfite preservative (E222) used to prevent browning and microbial growth. Like all sulfites it must be labelled above 10 mg/kg and can trigger reactions in sulfite-sensitive individuals.

descriptions.name: ble
descriptions.description_en: Whole wheat and wholemeal flour, keeping the bran and germ that refining removes. It supplies fibre, B vitamins, magnesium and plant protein, unlike white flour.

descriptions.name: bleu 1
descriptions.description_en: Brilliant Blue FCF (E133), a petroleum-derived synthetic dye. It is authorised in the EU and US, but the FDA is working to phase it out of the American food supply by the end of 2027.

descriptions.name: bleu 2
descriptions.description_en: Indigotine (E132), a synthetic blue dye made from petroleum. Authorised in the EU and US, it is among the six certified dyes the FDA is pushing manufacturers to remove.

descriptions.name: bœuf
descriptions.description_en: Unprocessed red meat and poultry — beef, pork, lamb, game and more. A complete source of protein, heme iron, zinc and vitamin B12, best eaten fresh rather than cured.

descriptions.name: bouillon
descriptions.description_en: Stock used as a flavour base. Homemade versions are nutritious, but industrial bouillon is usually dominated by salt, flavour enhancers and fat, with very little real meat or vegetable.

descriptions.name: BPA (Bisphénol A)
descriptions.description_en: A plastic and epoxy resin building block that leaches into food from can linings and containers. EFSA cut its tolerable daily intake 20,000-fold in 2023, and the EU banned it in food contact materials in 2025.

descriptions.name: brilliant black bn
descriptions.description_en: A synthetic black dye used in confectionery, sauces, decorations, and other processed foods. Some high-consuming children may approach or exceed the acceptable daily intake. Health: Frequent consumption of several products containing this dye can increase exposure beyond the level intended for daily use.

descriptions.name: bromate de potassium
descriptions.description_en: A flour improver (E924) classified IARC Group 2B, possibly carcinogenic. Banned in the EU, UK, Canada, Brazil and China, but still permitted in US bread. Residues can remain in the finished loaf.

descriptions.name: bronopol
descriptions.description_en: A preservative (2-bromo-2-nitropropane-1,3-diol) that slowly releases formaldehyde, an IARC Group 1 carcinogen. It is also a frequent cause of contact allergy, and its use in EU cosmetics is restricted.

descriptions.name: brown ht
descriptions.description_en: A synthetic brown dye used in bakery, dessert, and confectionery products. Exposure estimates have indicated that some high consumers, particularly children, may exceed the acceptable daily intake. Health: The main concern is repeated high intake from multiple colored products.

descriptions.name: butane
descriptions.description_en: Butane, isobutane and propane (E943/E944) used as propellants in aerosol food products such as cooking sprays and whipped cream. They are technical gases with no nutritional purpose.

descriptions.name: cabillaud
descriptions.description_en: White fish such as cod, hake, sea bass and trout. Lean, high in complete protein, iodine and selenium, and low in mercury compared with large predatory fish.

descriptions.name: cacao
descriptions.description_en: Pure cocoa and cocoa powder, among the most flavanol-rich foods known. Unsweetened cocoa supports vascular health and delivers magnesium and iron.

descriptions.name: cadmium
descriptions.description_en: A heavy metal that accumulates in the kidneys and bones over a lifetime. Cadmium and its compounds are IARC Group 1 human carcinogens, linked to lung cancer. It reaches food through polluted soil.

descriptions.name: cafe
descriptions.description_en: Coffee, one of the largest sources of antioxidants in the Western diet. Moderate consumption is associated with lower risk of type 2 diabetes and liver disease.

descriptions.name: cafeine
descriptions.description_en: A natural stimulant that improves alertness and physical performance. EFSA considers up to 400 mg a day safe for adults, but it disturbs sleep and should be limited in pregnancy.

descriptions.name: calcium benzoate
descriptions.description_en: A synthetic preservative that releases benzoate to slow microbial growth in acidic foods and drinks. It adds to total exposure from benzoic acid and other benzoates. Health: Sensitive individuals may experience hives or asthma-like reactions. High combined exposure should remain below the acceptable daily intake.

descriptions.name: calcium chloride
descriptions.description_en: A refined calcium salt used to firm vegetables, set cheese, and stabilize texture. Health: High concentrations can irritate the digestive tract and taste bitter, but normal authorized use is not considered a major health concern.

descriptions.name: calcium ferrocyanide
descriptions.description_en: A stable mineral complex used to keep salt and powders free-flowing. Health: No major safety concern is established at authorized use levels. The principal controls are dose and chemical purity.

descriptions.name: calcium gluconate
descriptions.description_en: A calcium salt used for firming, fortification, and stabilization. Health: Very high calcium intake can cause constipation and may be unsuitable for people with certain kidney or calcium-balance disorders.

descriptions.name: calcium hydroxide
descriptions.description_en: Also known as slaked lime, it is used to firm foods, process corn, and regulate acidity. Health: Concentrated material is irritating and alkaline. Excess residues could irritate the mouth or digestive tract, so processing controls are essential.

descriptions.name: calcium oxide
descriptions.description_en: Also called quicklime, it is a highly reactive industrial material used in controlled processing. It reacts to form less aggressive calcium compounds. Health: The raw powder is corrosive and can burn tissue. Finished food must not contain unsafe unreacted residues.

descriptions.name: calcium silicate
descriptions.description_en: A mineral anti-caking agent used in dry powders. Modern long-term toxicology data have been insufficient for a fully updated safety conclusion. Health: The concern is incomplete evidence on repeated exposure, not a proven disease effect at ordinary food levels.

descriptions.name: calcium sorbate
descriptions.description_en: A former preservative used to slow mold and yeast growth. It was withdrawn from the European Union food-additive list because the available data were insufficient to rule out a genotoxic concern. Health: Avoid products that list it as a food additive in markets where it is not authorized. Withdrawal reflects unresolved safety data, not proof that it causes cancer.

descriptions.name: calcium sulfate
descriptions.description_en: A mineral ingredient also known as food-grade gypsum, used for firming, flour treatment, and tofu production. Health: Very high intake can cause digestive discomfort or unnecessarily increase calcium exposure; normal food use is generally low risk.

descriptions.name: camphre
descriptions.description_en: An aromatic compound used in balms and decongestant rubs. It is effective in small amounts, but it is neurotoxic if swallowed and should never be applied to the face of infants or young children.

descriptions.name: cannelle
descriptions.description_en: Cinnamon, a spice with genuine research behind its effect on blood sugar regulation. Ceylon cinnamon is preferable to cassia for regular use, which contains more coumarin.

descriptions.name: canthaxanthin
descriptions.description_en: An orange-red carotenoid color with a low acceptable daily intake. Excessive exposure can cause canthaxanthin crystals to accumulate in the retina. Health: High intake may produce retinal deposits and visual changes. This is a genuine dose-related health concern and is why use is tightly restricted.

descriptions.name: caramel ammoniacal sulfite
descriptions.description_en: Caramel colour made with ammonia and sulfites (E150c/E150d). The process forms 4-methylimidazole, classified IARC Group 2B, possibly carcinogenic. EU rules cap its use, and California requires warning labelling above set levels.

descriptions.name: carbonate de calcium
descriptions.description_en: Calcium carbonate (E170), a mineral used as a white colour, anti-caking agent and calcium fortifier. It is simply chalk, and a genuine source of dietary calcium.

descriptions.name: Carbonate de magnésium
descriptions.description_en: Magnesium carbonate (E504), an anti-caking agent and acidity regulator that also contributes magnesium. It is a simple mineral salt, well tolerated at food levels.

descriptions.name: carbonate de sodium
descriptions.description_en: Sodium carbonate (E500), an acidity regulator and raising agent used in noodles, baked goods and cocoa. It is neutralised in the finished food but contributes sodium and marks industrial processing.

descriptions.name: carotenes
descriptions.description_en: Orange plant pigments (E160a) that the body converts to vitamin A. They are naturally present in carrots and other vegetables, and act as antioxidants as well as colours.

descriptions.name: carotte
descriptions.description_en: Carrots, one of the richest sources of beta-carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A. Fibre-rich and nutritious raw or cooked, with a little fat improving absorption.

descriptions.name: carraghenane
descriptions.description_en: A seaweed-derived thickener (E407) used in dairy, plant milks and processed meat. Food-grade carrageenan is authorised, but studies link it to gut inflammation and it is banned in EU infant formula.

descriptions.name: carraghenane degrade
descriptions.description_en: Degraded carrageenan, also called poligeenan, is the low-molecular-weight form and is classified IARC Group 2B, possibly carcinogenic. It has no authorised use as a food additive.

descriptions.name: caseinate
descriptions.description_en: Milk protein extracted with alkali and isolated from the rest of the dairy matrix. It is a purely technical ingredient used to bind and emulsify, and marks an industrially assembled recipe.

descriptions.name: caviar
descriptions.description_en: Fish roe, dense in omega-3, vitamin B12 and vitamin D. Genuinely nutritious, though naturally salty, so portions stay small.

descriptions.name: cellulose
descriptions.description_en: Plant cellulose (E460), used as an anti-caking agent and bulking fibre. It is not digested and behaves as insoluble fibre, but in processed food it usually replaces real ingredients.

descriptions.name: ceramides
descriptions.description_en: Lipids that naturally make up the skin's protective barrier. Applied topically they help restore that barrier and reduce water loss, with strong evidence behind them and virtually no irritation risk.

descriptions.name: ceteareth
descriptions.description_en: An ethoxylated emulsifier used to blend oil and water. The ethoxylation process can leave traces of 1,4-dioxane, a possible carcinogen, so manufacturers are expected to purify it out.

descriptions.name: champignon
descriptions.description_en: Mushrooms of all kinds, from button to shiitake and porcini. They provide B vitamins, selenium and beta-glucans, and are one of the few plant sources of vitamin D when sun-exposed.

descriptions.name: charbon vegetal
descriptions.description_en: Vegetable carbon (E153), a black colourant made by carbonising plant material. It is authorised in the EU but adds no nutritional value and can bind medicines and nutrients in the gut.

descriptions.name: cheddar deshydrate
descriptions.description_en: Cheese powder used to coat crisps and season mixes. It is very high in sodium and often blended with flavour enhancers and anti-caking agents rather than being simply dried cheese.

descriptions.name: chlorophylle
descriptions.description_en: Green plant pigments (E140/E141) used as colouring. The natural form is benign; the copper-stabilised version used for brighter colour adds a small amount of copper to the diet.

descriptions.name: chlorpyrifos
descriptions.description_en: An organophosphate insecticide banned across the EU since 2020. EFSA could not establish a safe exposure level, citing genotoxicity concerns and evidence of harm to brain development in children.

descriptions.name: chocolat noir
descriptions.description_en: Dark chocolate at 70% cocoa and above. The higher the cocoa content, the more flavanols and minerals and the less sugar — genuinely beneficial in reasonable portions.

descriptions.name: chocolat non sucre
descriptions.description_en: Unsweetened 100% chocolate, pure cocoa mass with no added sugar. It is the most nutrient-dense form of chocolate, rich in flavanols, magnesium and fibre.

descriptions.name: chorizo
descriptions.description_en: A cured, paprika-spiced sausage. As a processed meat it falls under the IARC Group 1 classification: the curing and smoking process generates compounds tied to colorectal cancer.

descriptions.name: chou-fleur
descriptions.description_en: Cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, kale and fermented cabbage such as sauerkraut and kimchi. Cruciferous vegetables rich in fibre, vitamin C and glucosinolates; the fermented forms add live cultures.

descriptions.name: Chrome hexavalent (Cr VI)
descriptions.description_en: Chromium(VI) compounds are IARC Group 1 human carcinogens, causally linked to lung and nasal cancer. An industrial contaminant, notably from tanning and plating, with no legitimate use in consumer products.

descriptions.name: cire d abeille
descriptions.description_en: Beeswax (E901), a natural glazing agent used to coat sweets and fruit. It is not absorbed by the body and is one of the simplest coatings available.

descriptions.name: cire de candelilla
descriptions.description_en: A plant wax (E902) from a Mexican shrub, used to glaze sweets and coatings. It is not absorbed, and it is a vegan alternative to beeswax and shellac.

descriptions.name: cire de carnauba
descriptions.description_en: A glazing wax (E903) from Brazilian palm leaves, used to shine sweets, chewing gum and coated tablets. It is not absorbed by the body, but it is a purely cosmetic industrial coating.

descriptions.name: cire microcristalline
descriptions.description_en: A petroleum-derived wax (E905) used as a glazing and release agent. It is not absorbed by the body, but it originates from mineral oil refining rather than from a plant or animal source.

descriptions.name: cmc
descriptions.description_en: Carboxymethylcellulose (E466), a synthetic thickener made from cellulose. A controlled human trial found it altered the gut microbiome and intestinal lining, and it is a strong marker of ultra-processed food.

descriptions.name: coal tar
descriptions.description_en: A by-product of coal processing, historically used in anti-dandruff and psoriasis treatments and in dyes. Coal tars are IARC Group 1 human carcinogens; untreated preparations are restricted in EU cosmetics.

descriptions.name: cochenille
descriptions.description_en: Carmine (E120), a red colour made from crushed cochineal insects. It is natural rather than synthetic, but it is a recognised allergen that has caused severe reactions, and it is not vegetarian.

descriptions.name: collagene
descriptions.description_en: A protein used in skincare as a surface moisturiser. Its molecules are too large to penetrate the skin, so it hydrates and softens rather than rebuilding collagen — but it is harmless and well tolerated.

descriptions.name: Colorants azoïques textiles
descriptions.description_en: Textile azo dyes that can break down on the skin into benzidine and related aromatic amines, IARC Group 1 human carcinogens. Banned in the EU in textiles designed for prolonged skin contact.

descriptions.name: concentre de fruits
descriptions.description_en: Fruit or vegetable juice boiled down to concentrate its sugars. Manufacturers use it to sweeten products while keeping a natural-sounding label; the fibre is gone and the sugar behaves like added sugar.

descriptions.name: coriandre
descriptions.description_en: Fresh herbs including coriander, parsley, dill, mint, sage and bay. They add flavour without salt or sugar and carry concentrated antioxidants and essential oils.

descriptions.name: cornichon naturel
descriptions.description_en: Naturally lacto-fermented vegetables, kombucha and kvass. Fermentation creates live bacteria and organic acids that support gut health, with no additives needed.

descriptions.name: couscous complet
descriptions.description_en: Whole couscous, freekeh, farro and pearled barley. Minimally refined grains that keep their fibre and minerals, giving slow-release energy rather than a sugar spike.

descriptions.name: creme
descriptions.description_en: Cream and crème fraîche, a simple dairy fat with no additives. Rich in saturated fat and calories, so a genuine ingredient best used in modest amounts.

descriptions.name: crevette
descriptions.description_en: Shellfish, molluscs and seaweed. Rich in protein, zinc, selenium and iodine, and low in fat; seaweed adds minerals but can be very high in iodine.

descriptions.name: curcuma
descriptions.description_en: Turmeric, whose curcumin has well-documented anti-inflammatory activity. Absorption is poor on its own, which is why traditional recipes pair it with black pepper and fat.

descriptions.name: curcumine
descriptions.description_en: The yellow pigment of turmeric (E100), used as a natural colour. It carries genuine anti-inflammatory activity, though the amounts used for colouring are far below any therapeutic dose.

descriptions.name: cyanocobalamine
descriptions.description_en: A stable added form of vitamin B12, widely used in fortified foods and supplements and important for anyone eating little animal produce. Safe at normal intake; it marks a fortified rather than naturally rich product.

descriptions.name: cyclamate
descriptions.description_en: An artificial sweetener (E952) still permitted in the EU but banned in the US since 1969 after bladder tumours appeared in rats. It has one of the lowest acceptable daily intakes of any sweetener.

descriptions.name: Cyclopentasiloxane D5
descriptions.description_en: A silicone that gives cosmetics a smooth, fast-drying feel. It is classified as very persistent and very bioaccumulative under EU chemical law, and its use in cosmetics is restricted in Europe.

descriptions.name: cyclosiloxane
descriptions.description_en: Cyclic silicones (cyclomethicone, D4, D5, D6) used for silky texture in hair and skin products. They are persistent in the environment and are progressively being restricted in EU cosmetics.

descriptions.name: Cyclotétrasiloxane D4
descriptions.description_en: A cyclic silicone classified in the EU as toxic to reproduction and as persistent and bioaccumulative. Its use in cosmetics is restricted in Europe, starting with rinse-off products.

descriptions.name: d-alpha tocopherol
descriptions.description_en: Vitamin E used as a natural antioxidant (E306–E309) to stop fats going rancid. It is beneficial and among the most benign additives, though the added form is an isolated industrial extract.

descriptions.name: datem
descriptions.description_en: DATEM (E472e), a dough strengthener in industrial bread. EFSA found no safety concern in 2020, but laboratory work links it to gut microbiome disruption and a large French cohort tied higher intake to slightly raised type 2 diabetes risk.

descriptions.name: DEA (Diéthanolamine)
descriptions.description_en: A foaming and pH-adjusting agent that can react with nitrites to form nitrosamines. Diethanolamine is prohibited in cosmetics in the European Union.

descriptions.name: defatted soy flour
descriptions.description_en: Soy flour with the oil removed by industrial solvent extraction, then used as a cheap protein filler. It is a highly processed commodity ingredient with little resemblance to whole soy.

descriptions.name: delta-tocopherol
descriptions.description_en: A natural vitamin E form (E309) and one of the most effective tocopherols at stopping oils going rancid. Plant-derived and nutritionally useful.

descriptions.name: dextrine
descriptions.description_en: A partially broken-down starch used as a thickener, binder and bulking agent. It is a refined carbohydrate with a high glycemic response and no nutrients.

descriptions.name: dextrose
descriptions.description_en: Industrially refined pure glucose, usually from corn starch. Absorbed very rapidly, it causes sharp blood-sugar and insulin spikes with no nutritional benefit.

descriptions.name: diazolidinyl urea
descriptions.description_en: A cosmetic preservative that works by slowly releasing formaldehyde, an IARC Group 1 human carcinogen. It is a known contact allergen and its use is capped under EU cosmetics rules.

descriptions.name: diglutamate de calcium
descriptions.description_en: A flavour enhancer (E623) used as a lower-sodium alternative to MSG. Considered safe at food levels, but it signals a product engineered on additives rather than ingredients.

descriptions.name: diglutamate de magnesium
descriptions.description_en: A flavour enhancer (E625) from the glutamate family, used to boost savoury taste in processed foods. Safe at normal intake, but characteristic of heavily seasoned industrial products.

descriptions.name: Diméthylformamide (DMF)
descriptions.description_en: An industrial solvent used in synthetic leather and coatings. It is classified as toxic to reproduction in the EU and is restricted under REACH, with strict limits on residues in consumer articles.

descriptions.name: dimethylpolysiloxane
descriptions.description_en: A silicone anti-foaming agent (E900) used mainly in frying oils and industrial cooking. It is inert and poorly absorbed, but it is a synthetic silicone typical of large-scale food production.

descriptions.name: dioxines
descriptions.description_en: Persistent industrial by-products that accumulate in animal fat and reach us mainly through meat, dairy and fish. TCDD is an IARC Group 1 human carcinogen, and EFSA cut the tolerable weekly intake sevenfold in 2018.

descriptions.name: dioxyde de carbone
descriptions.description_en: Carbon dioxide (E290), used to carbonate drinks and to protect packaged food from oxidation. It is inert at food levels and leaves nothing behind.

descriptions.name: dioxyde de soufre
descriptions.description_en: A preservative and antioxidant (E220) common in wine, dried fruit and processed potato. It must be declared as an allergen in the EU above 10 mg/kg because it can trigger asthma attacks in sensitive people.

descriptions.name: dioxyde de titane
descriptions.description_en: A white colouring (E171) used in sweets, sauces and supplements. Banned as a food additive across the EU since August 2022 after EFSA could not rule out DNA damage. Still allowed in the US and in cosmetics.

descriptions.name: diphosphate
descriptions.description_en: Diphosphates (E450) used as raising agents and to retain water in meat and seafood. They add to total phosphate intake, which EFSA capped in 2019 over cardiovascular and kidney concerns.

descriptions.name: dmdm hydantoin
descriptions.description_en: One of the most common formaldehyde-releasing preservatives in shampoos and lotions. The formaldehyde it emits is an IARC Group 1 human carcinogen; EU rules restrict its level and require warning labelling.

descriptions.name: eau
descriptions.description_en: Water, plain or sparkling — the only drink the body genuinely needs. It carries no calories, sugar or additives, and adequate intake supports every function in the body.

descriptions.name: Eau de Javel (hypochlorite)
descriptions.description_en: Sodium hypochlorite bleach, an effective disinfectant that is corrosive to skin, eyes and airways. Mixed with ammonia or acidic cleaners it releases toxic gases, and it should never be combined with other products.

descriptions.name: edta
descriptions.description_en: A synthetic chelator (E385) that traps metal ions to stop fats going rancid and colours fading. Authorised at limited levels, it can also bind minerals the body needs and does not occur in nature.

descriptions.name: epeautre
descriptions.description_en: Spelt, an ancient wheat variety richer in protein and minerals than modern wheat. It still contains gluten, but many find it easier to digest.

descriptions.name: epinard
descriptions.description_en: Spinach, a leafy green exceptionally dense in folate, vitamin K, magnesium, plant iron and lutein. Its oxalates slightly limit calcium and iron absorption, which cooking and a source of vitamin C largely offset.

descriptions.name: erythorbate de sodium
descriptions.description_en: An antioxidant (E316) that is a mirror-image form of vitamin C, used to keep cured meat pink and fats fresh. It is safe, but it has no vitamin activity and appears mostly in processed meat.

descriptions.name: erythritol
descriptions.description_en: A fermented and purified sugar alcohol used as a low-calorie sweetener. Large single doses can cause diarrhea, nausea, bloating, or abdominal discomfort. Health: EFSA confirmed a laxative threshold. Studies have reported cardiovascular associations, but a causal health risk from normal food consumption has not been established.

descriptions.name: esters acetiques
descriptions.description_en: Acetic acid esters of mono- and diglycerides (E472a), an emulsifier used to stabilise fats in industrial baking and desserts. EFSA raised no safety concern, but it is a purely technical ingredient.

descriptions.name: esters citriques
descriptions.description_en: Citric acid esters of mono- and diglycerides (E472c), used to emulsify and prevent oxidation. EFSA found no safety concern, though it marks an industrially assembled recipe.

descriptions.name: esters de propylene glycol
descriptions.description_en: Propylene glycol esters of fatty acids (E477), used to aerate whipped toppings and cake mixes. Permitted at capped levels, and characteristic of ultra-processed desserts.

descriptions.name: esters de sucrose
descriptions.description_en: Sucrose esters of fatty acids (E473), synthetic emulsifiers built from sugar and fat. They are authorised at limited levels but belong to the emulsifier family under study for effects on the gut lining.

descriptions.name: esters lactiques
descriptions.description_en: Lactic acid esters of mono- and diglycerides (E472b), used to aerate whipped and baked products. Considered safe by EFSA, it is a chemically modified fat with no nutritional role.

descriptions.name: esters polyglyceriques
descriptions.description_en: Polyglycerol esters of fatty acids (E475), used to emulsify cakes, ice cream and spreads. Permitted at capped levels, and a clear marker of ultra-processed formulation.

descriptions.name: ethyl paraben
descriptions.description_en: A synthetic paraben preservative used to prevent mold and bacterial growth. Experimental research has examined weak hormone-like activity, so exposure is controlled through a combined acceptable daily intake. Health: No cancer claim is justified at authorized food levels. The relevant concern is repeated combined exposure to several parabens.

descriptions.name: ethylcellulose
descriptions.description_en: A modified cellulose (E462) used as a binder and film former. It is indigestible and considered safe, serving a purely technical role in manufacturing.

descriptions.name: ethylparaben
descriptions.description_en: A preservative (E214/E215) permitted in a narrow range of EU foods. Parabens have weak oestrogen-like activity in laboratory studies; the ethyl form is among the least potent of the family.

descriptions.name: eucheuma transforme
descriptions.description_en: Processed eucheuma seaweed (E407a), a cheaper, less purified relative of carrageenan. It shares carrageenan's concerns about gut inflammation and is banned in EU infant formula.

descriptions.name: extrait de paprika
descriptions.description_en: A red-orange colouring (E160c) extracted from peppers, carrying capsanthin and carotenoids. It is a plant-derived colour with antioxidant activity.

descriptions.name: Extrait de romarin
descriptions.description_en: Rosemary extract (E392), a plant-based antioxidant increasingly used to replace synthetic preservatives such as BHA and BHT. It is rich in natural polyphenols.

descriptions.name: farine de ble enrichie
descriptions.description_en: White flour with a few vitamins and iron added back after refining stripped them out. The fortification helps, but the fibre and most micronutrients of the whole grain are gone for good.

descriptions.name: fatty acids
descriptions.description_en: Refined fatty acids used as processing aids, glazing agents, or anti-caking agents. The E-number does not identify a single harmful fat. Health: Health impact depends more on the source and overall fat profile of the food than on this additive function.

descriptions.name: fécule de maïs
descriptions.description_en: Cornstarch extracted industrially, often from GM corn outside the EU. A refined carbohydrate with a high glycemic index and no fibre, vitamins or minerals.

descriptions.name: fécule de tapioca
descriptions.description_en: Starch from the cassava root, used as a gluten-free thickener. It is a refined starch with little nutrition of its own, but a clean, single-ingredient alternative to modified starches.

descriptions.name: ferments lactiques
descriptions.description_en: Live bacterial cultures such as lactobacillus and bifidobacterium. They ferment the food, make it more digestible, and contribute to a healthy gut microbiome.

descriptions.name: ferrocyanure de potassium
descriptions.description_en: An anti-caking agent (E536) added to salt to keep it free-flowing. Despite the name, the cyanide is locked in a stable complex and EFSA considers it safe at permitted levels.

descriptions.name: ferrocyanure de sodium
descriptions.description_en: An anti-caking agent (E535) added to table salt to keep it free-flowing. Despite the alarming name, the cyanide is locked in a stable complex and EFSA considers it safe at permitted levels.

descriptions.name: ferrous gluconate
descriptions.description_en: An iron salt used to darken olives and provide iron. It can significantly increase iron exposure in concentrated products. Health: Excess iron can cause nausea, constipation, abdominal pain, and oxidative injury. It is especially dangerous in large accidental doses to children.

descriptions.name: ferrous lactate
descriptions.description_en: An iron salt used mainly to stabilize the dark color of olives and other foods. Health: Too much iron may cause digestive symptoms and is unsuitable for people with iron-overload disorders.

descriptions.name: feta
descriptions.description_en: Traditional brined and firm cheeses such as feta, halloumi, manchego and paneer. Simple, minimally processed cheeses rich in protein and calcium, though high in salt.

descriptions.name: feuille de kaffir
descriptions.description_en: Aromatic ingredients such as kaffir lime leaf, lemongrass, galangal, fresh ginger, wasabi and horseradish. Whole aromatics with antibacterial and antioxidant compounds, used in small amounts.

descriptions.name: fibre de racine de manioc
descriptions.description_en: Cassava root fibre, a whole-plant source of resistant starch that feeds beneficial gut bacteria. It acts as prebiotic fibre rather than a refined additive.

descriptions.name: figue
descriptions.description_en: Figs, dates and raisins — dried fruits concentrated in sugar but also in fibre, potassium and minerals. Genuinely nutritious, though the sugar density means smaller portions.

descriptions.name: foie
descriptions.description_en: Liver and other organ meats, the most nutrient-dense animal foods there are. Liver is exceptionally rich in vitamin A, B12 and iron — so rich that weekly rather than daily intake is advised.

descriptions.name: formaldehyde
descriptions.description_en: A preservative and disinfectant classified IARC Group 1 human carcinogen, causally linked to nasopharyngeal cancer and leukaemia. Banned as a direct food additive and prohibited in EU cosmetics.

descriptions.name: fragrance
descriptions.description_en: A single word hiding a mixture that can contain dozens of undisclosed compounds. EU law requires 26 known fragrance allergens to be named separately, which is why perfumed products are a leading cause of contact allergy.

descriptions.name: fraise
descriptions.description_en: Strawberries, blueberries and raspberries — among the most antioxidant-dense fruits, high in vitamin C and polyphenols while being low in sugar. Excellent eaten regularly.

descriptions.name: fromage
descriptions.description_en: Real cheese, made by curdling milk with rennet or cultures. It concentrates protein and calcium, but also salt and saturated fat, so portion size matters.

descriptions.name: fromage allege
descriptions.description_en: Reduced-fat cheese. Lower in calories, but manufacturers often compensate with added salt, starch or stabilisers, and the texture depends on more processing than full-fat cheese.

descriptions.name: fromage fondu
descriptions.description_en: Processed cheese made by melting cheese scraps with emulsifying salts, usually phosphates. It is high in sodium and phosphate additives and bears little resemblance to traditionally made cheese.

descriptions.name: fructose
descriptions.description_en: Isolated fructose, very different from the fructose inside whole fruit, which comes with fibre and nutrients. It is metabolised by the liver and, in isolated form, promotes fat accumulation there.

descriptions.name: Fructose ajouté
descriptions.description_en: Fructose added in isolated form, without the fibre and nutrients of whole fruit. It is processed almost entirely by the liver, and regular intake is linked to fat accumulation there.

descriptions.name: fruit
descriptions.description_en: Whole fruits and vegetables, the foundation of a healthy diet. They deliver fibre, vitamins, minerals and antioxidants in their natural matrix, with no processing needed to be good for you.

descriptions.name: Fruit du moine / Monk fruit
descriptions.description_en: A plant-derived sweetener from monk fruit, free of calories and with no effect on blood sugar. One of the better options for replacing sugar, though it is a concentrated extract.

descriptions.name: fumee naturelle
descriptions.description_en: Smoke flavouring produced by condensing wood smoke. It can carry polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, which is why EFSA has re-evaluated smoke flavourings and the EU has restricted several of them.

descriptions.name: gallates
descriptions.description_en: Propyl, octyl and dodecyl gallate (E310–E312), synthetic antioxidants that stop fats going rancid. They are permitted at low levels but can trigger contact allergy and are restricted in foods for infants.

descriptions.name: gamma-tocopherol
descriptions.description_en: A natural form of vitamin E (E308) used to prevent fats oxidising. It is a plant-derived antioxidant with genuine nutritional value.

descriptions.name: garlic
descriptions.description_en: A whole food valued for allicin, its sulphur compound with antibacterial and cardiovascular activity. Crushing it and letting it rest a few minutes before cooking preserves more of that compound.

descriptions.name: gelatine
descriptions.description_en: Collagen extracted from animal skin and bone by acid or alkali treatment. It is a safe, protein-based gelling agent, though of animal origin and low in nutritional value.

descriptions.name: gelatine e441
descriptions.description_en: Collagen extracted from animal skin and bone by acid or alkali treatment (E441). It is a safe, protein-based gelling agent, though of animal origin with little nutritional value.

descriptions.name: gelée royale
descriptions.description_en: Bee products including royal jelly, propolis and pollen. They contain a range of natural compounds, though evidence for their claimed benefits is limited and they can trigger allergies.

descriptions.name: ghee
descriptions.description_en: Clarified butter with the milk solids removed, leaving almost pure fat. It is very stable for high-heat cooking and virtually lactose-free, though still rich in saturated fat.

descriptions.name: gingembre
descriptions.description_en: Ginger, valued for its gingerols, which have anti-inflammatory properties and a well-evidenced effect on nausea. A whole root used fresh, dried or infused.

descriptions.name: ginseng
descriptions.description_en: Ginseng root, traditionally used to support energy and resistance to fatigue. Research on ginsenosides is promising though still limited; it can interact with some medications.

descriptions.name: gluconic acid
descriptions.description_en: An organic acid produced from glucose and used to regulate acidity or bind minerals. Health: It has low toxicity, although concentrated or high amounts may irritate the digestive system.

descriptions.name: glucono-delta-lactone
descriptions.description_en: A glucose-derived compound that slowly releases gluconic acid, helping set tofu, cure foods, and control acidity. Health: Large amounts may cause bloating, gas, or digestive discomfort.

descriptions.name: glucose
descriptions.description_en: Added glucose in isolated form, absorbed almost instantly. It raises blood sugar faster than table sugar and carries no nutritional value beyond calories.

descriptions.name: glutamate monoammonique
descriptions.description_en: A glutamate flavour enhancer (E624) that intensifies umami in industrial seasonings. It performs the same role as MSG under a different name.

descriptions.name: glutamate monopotassique
descriptions.description_en: A flavour enhancer (E622) from the glutamate family, used like MSG to build savoury taste with less real ingredient. It is a reliable marker of ultra-processed food.

descriptions.name: glyceryl diacetate (diacetin)
descriptions.description_en: A manufactured glycerol ester used to carry flavors, retain moisture, and improve processing. Health: It is broken down into glycerol and acetic acid. Modern long-term data are less extensive than for some common additives, but no major risk is established at permitted use.

descriptions.name: glycine
descriptions.description_en: An amino acid (E640) used as a mild sweetener and flavour modifier. The body makes its own supply, and it is safe at the small amounts used in food.

descriptions.name: glyphosate
descriptions.description_en: The world's most used herbicide, found as a residue in cereals and legumes. IARC classified it Group 2A, probably carcinogenic to humans, in 2015, though EFSA reached a different conclusion.

descriptions.name: gomme adragante
descriptions.description_en: A plant gum (E413) from the astragalus shrub, used as a thickener and stabiliser. It behaves as soluble fibre and is well tolerated, though it can cause bloating in quantity.

descriptions.name: gomme arabique
descriptions.description_en: Acacia gum (E414), a tree sap used as a stabiliser. It is a prebiotic soluble fibre that feeds gut bacteria, and one of the oldest and gentlest additives in use.

descriptions.name: gomme cassia
descriptions.description_en: A thickener (E427) from cassia tree seeds, authorised in the EU with strict purity limits because the raw seed contains natural anthraquinones. Purified food grade is considered safe.

descriptions.name: Goudron de houille (coal tar)
descriptions.description_en: A thick residue from coal distillation used in some medicated shampoos and dyes. Coal tars are IARC Group 1 human carcinogens; untreated forms are restricted in EU cosmetic products.

descriptions.name: graines
descriptions.description_en: Mixed seeds, a concentrated source of plant protein, fibre, minerals and healthy fats. They add real nutritional density to bread, salads and yoghurt.

descriptions.name: graines de chia
descriptions.description_en: Chia seeds, exceptionally high in soluble fibre and omega-3 ALA. They absorb many times their weight in liquid, which helps satiety and digestive regularity.

descriptions.name: graines de courge
descriptions.description_en: Pumpkin, poppy, fennel, coriander, mustard, nigella and hemp seeds. All are dense in minerals — pumpkin seeds especially in magnesium and zinc — along with protein and healthy fats.

descriptions.name: graines de lin
descriptions.description_en: Flax seeds, one of the richest plant sources of omega-3 ALA and lignans. They need to be ground to be absorbed — whole seeds pass through largely intact.

descriptions.name: graines de sesame
descriptions.description_en: Sesame seeds, remarkably high in calcium, magnesium and lignans. They are more nutritious hulled or ground, as in tahini, than left whole.

descriptions.name: graines de tournesol
descriptions.description_en: Sunflower seeds, an excellent source of vitamin E, magnesium and selenium. Nutritious as a whole food, though high in omega-6, so best balanced with omega-3 sources.

descriptions.name: graisse interesterifiee
descriptions.description_en: Fat rearranged chemically or enzymatically to replace trans fats and mimic their texture. It avoids trans fats but remains a laboratory-restructured fat, and its long-term metabolic effects are still debated.

descriptions.name: gras trans
descriptions.description_en: Trans fatty acids raise bad cholesterol while lowering the good kind, directly increasing cardiovascular risk. The WHO has called for their global elimination and there is no safe level of intake.

descriptions.name: green s
descriptions.description_en: A synthetic green food dye used to create or intensify color. It has an acceptable daily intake, and high consumption of several colored products can increase total exposure. Health: The concern is unnecessary cumulative exposure and possible intolerance in sensitive individuals, not proven carcinogenicity.

descriptions.name: grenade
descriptions.description_en: Pomegranate, kiwi and melons. Pomegranate is exceptionally rich in punicalagins and antioxidants, while kiwi delivers more vitamin C per gram than most citrus.

descriptions.name: guarana
descriptions.description_en: A South American seed with a high natural caffeine content, released more slowly than coffee. The plant is natural, but the energy drinks it appears in usually are not.

descriptions.name: haricots
descriptions.description_en: Beans of all kinds, a staple source of plant protein, resistant starch and fibre. Their slow-release carbohydrate makes them one of the best foods for stable blood sugar.

descriptions.name: helium
descriptions.description_en: An inert gas used in specialized packaging or processing. It leaves no meaningful chemical residue in food. Health: Food use is not considered a safety concern. Inhalation of pressurized helium is a separate non-food hazard.

descriptions.name: hijiki
descriptions.description_en: A brown seaweed that accumulates unusually high levels of inorganic arsenic, a known human carcinogen. Food agencies in the UK, Canada and Ireland advise avoiding it and choosing other seaweeds instead.

descriptions.name: Huile de canola / colza raffinée
descriptions.description_en: Refined rapeseed oil with a favourable fatty acid profile on paper. High-heat refining degrades its omega-3 content and generates process contaminants; cold-pressed versions are better.

descriptions.name: huile de coco
descriptions.description_en: Virgin coconut oil, cold-pressed and unrefined. It is stable for cooking and rich in medium-chain fats, but also very high in saturated fat, so it deserves moderation.

descriptions.name: huile de coco modifiee
descriptions.description_en: Coconut oil that has been hydrogenated, fractionated or interesterified to change its melting point. These industrial treatments alter the fat structure and mark a heavily engineered product.

descriptions.name: huile de colza
descriptions.description_en: Rapeseed (canola) oil, favourable in fatty acid profile but industrially refined at high heat, which degrades its omega-3 content and forms process contaminants. Cold-pressed versions are a better choice.

descriptions.name: huile de coton
descriptions.description_en: Cottonseed oil, extracted from a non-food crop that is heavily treated with pesticides. It is very high in omega-6 fats and requires intensive refining to remove natural toxins such as gossypol.

descriptions.name: huile de lin
descriptions.description_en: Flaxseed oil, the richest plant source of omega-3 ALA. It oxidises very easily, so it must be kept cold, used raw, and never heated.

descriptions.name: huile de mais
descriptions.description_en: Corn oil, an industrially refined oil very high in omega-6 fatty acids. An unbalanced omega-6 to omega-3 ratio is associated with chronic inflammation when consumed regularly.

descriptions.name: huile de noix
descriptions.description_en: Walnut oil, rich in omega-3 ALA and polyphenols. Best used cold on salads, as heat destroys its delicate fatty acids.

descriptions.name: huile de palme
descriptions.description_en: A cheap refined fat used across industrial food. High-temperature refining forms 3-MCPD and glycidyl esters — glycidol is rated IARC Group 2A, probably carcinogenic — and EFSA set very low tolerable intakes. Also a major driver of deforestation.

descriptions.name: huile de pepin de raisin
descriptions.description_en: Grapeseed oil, extracted from winemaking residue and usually solvent-refined. It is very high in omega-6 fats, which tilts the diet away from omega-3 balance when used regularly.

descriptions.name: huile de sesame
descriptions.description_en: Sesame oil, rich in antioxidants such as sesamol which make it unusually stable. Toasted versions are for flavour; both are traditional whole-seed oils.

descriptions.name: huile de soja
descriptions.description_en: The most widely used oil in industrial food, refined at high heat and dominated by omega-6 fats. It is often derived from GM crops outside the EU and contributes to an inflammatory fatty acid balance.

descriptions.name: huile de tournesol
descriptions.description_en: Sunflower oil, usually refined and very high in omega-6 fats. It oxidises readily when heated, generating harmful compounds, and its regular use tilts the diet away from omega-3 balance.

descriptions.name: Huile hydrogénée / Gras trans
descriptions.description_en: Partially hydrogenated oil, the main industrial source of trans fats. Trans fats raise LDL cholesterol and lower HDL; the WHO calls for their elimination and the EU caps them at 2% of total fat.

descriptions.name: Huile minérale (paraffinum, petrolatum)
descriptions.description_en: Petroleum-derived oils used in creams, balms and lubricants. Untreated and mildly treated mineral oils are IARC Group 1 human carcinogens; refined cosmetic grades are safer but can still carry aromatic hydrocarbon (MOAH) residues.

descriptions.name: huile vegetale
descriptions.description_en: An unspecified blend, most often refined palm or rapeseed. The label hides which fat is actually used, and heavy industrial refining is typical of ultra-processed food that whole ingredients never require.

descriptions.name: Huile végétale (non spécifiée)
descriptions.description_en: An undisclosed blend of refined oils, most often palm or rapeseed. The label hides which fat is actually used, which alone makes it worth limiting.

descriptions.name: huile vegetale bromee
descriptions.description_en: Brominated vegetable oil, used to keep citrus flavours suspended in soft drinks. The FDA revoked its authorisation in 2024 after evidence of thyroid harm and bromine build-up in body fat. Long banned in the EU, UK and Japan.

descriptions.name: hydrochloric acid
descriptions.description_en: A strong processing acid used in controlled amounts to adjust pH or manufacture ingredients. It is neutralized or highly diluted in the finished food. Health: The concentrated industrial chemical is corrosive, but that hazard should not be confused with properly controlled residues in food.

descriptions.name: hydrogen
descriptions.description_en: A gas used in limited food-processing applications. It is highly flammable during industrial handling but does not remain as a toxic food residue. Health: The main hazard is fire or explosion during manufacturing, not consumption of properly processed food.

descriptions.name: hydrogenated
descriptions.description_en: Oil hardened by adding hydrogen to extend shelf life. Partial hydrogenation creates trans fats, which are strongly linked to heart disease and are now restricted in the EU and banned in the US.

descriptions.name: hydroquinone
descriptions.description_en: A powerful skin-lightening agent. Banned in EU cosmetics except for limited professional nail products, because it causes irreversible skin discolouration (ochronosis) and carries genotoxicity concerns.

descriptions.name: hydroxyde de calcium
descriptions.description_en: Calcium hydroxide (E526), or slaked lime, used to treat corn (nixtamalisation) and adjust acidity. Harmless in the finished food, but corrosive in raw form and a sign of industrial processing.

descriptions.name: hydroxyde de potassium
descriptions.description_en: Potassium hydroxide (E525), a strongly alkaline processing aid used to adjust acidity and treat cocoa. It is neutralised in the final product but marks a chemically processed recipe.

descriptions.name: hydroxyde de sodium
descriptions.description_en: Sodium hydroxide (E524), caustic soda, used to adjust pH and to peel or treat foods such as pretzels and olives. Corrosive in concentrated form; its presence indicates industrial processing.

descriptions.name: hydroxypropyl starch
descriptions.description_en: A chemically modified starch that remains stable during freezing, heating, and storage. Health: No major specific harm is established at permitted use. Frequent presence indicates a highly engineered texture.

descriptions.name: imidazolidinyl urea
descriptions.description_en: A widely used cosmetic preservative that releases formaldehyde, an IARC Group 1 human carcinogen. It is a recognised contact allergen and is restricted under EU cosmetics regulation.

descriptions.name: imitation mozzarella
descriptions.description_en: A cheese substitute built from vegetable oil, starch and milk proteins rather than curdled milk. It is engineered for melt and cost, and delivers none of the qualities of real cheese.

descriptions.name: inositol
descriptions.description_en: A sugar-like compound found naturally in fruits, beans and grains, and also produced by the body. Added to energy drinks and supplements, it is well tolerated, but the added form is more marketing than nutritional need.

descriptions.name: inuline
descriptions.description_en: A prebiotic fibre from chicory root that feeds beneficial gut bacteria. Genuinely useful for digestive health, though large amounts can cause bloating in sensitive people.

descriptions.name: irradiation
descriptions.description_en: Treatment with ionising radiation to kill microbes and extend shelf life. It leaves no radioactivity and is authorised in the EU for a narrow list of foods, which must carry an "irradiated" label; it does degrade some vitamins.

descriptions.name: isolat de proteines
descriptions.description_en: Protein stripped from its original food by industrial extraction, leaving no fibre, fat or micronutrients. Useful for boosting protein figures on a label, but a marker of a reconstructed product.

descriptions.name: Isolat de protéines (whey, soja, lait)
descriptions.description_en: Protein separated from its original food by industrial processing, leaving no fibre, fat or micronutrients. Effective for raising protein figures, but a marker of a reconstructed product.

descriptions.name: isomalt
descriptions.description_en: A polyol (E953) made from sucrose, common in sugar-free sweets. It does not feed tooth decay and has a low glycemic impact, but it causes digestive upset in larger amounts.

descriptions.name: isopropyl myristate
descriptions.description_en: A synthetic emollient that gives creams a light, fast-absorbing feel. It is not toxic, but it is highly comedogenic and a common trigger of clogged pores in acne-prone skin.

descriptions.name: Isothiazolinones (MIT, CMIT)
descriptions.description_en: Preservatives in cosmetics, paints and household products, and among the strongest contact allergens known. Methylisothiazolinone has been banned from leave-on cosmetics in the EU since 2017 after a wave of skin reactions.

descriptions.name: jambon
descriptions.description_en: Cured or cooked pork leg. As a processed meat it falls under the IARC Group 1 classification (2015): salting and nitrite curing generate compounds that raise colorectal cancer risk with regular intake.

descriptions.name: jaune 6
descriptions.description_en: Sunset Yellow (E110), a synthetic azo dye. EU law requires a warning that it may affect children's activity and attention, and the FDA is phasing it out of US foods.

descriptions.name: jaune de quinoléine
descriptions.description_en: Quinoline Yellow (E104), a synthetic dye carrying the mandatory EU warning about effects on children's activity and attention. It is not authorised as a food colour in the United States.

descriptions.name: jerky
descriptions.description_en: Salted and dried strips of beef. It counts as processed meat, an IARC Group 1 human carcinogen, and is also very high in sodium. Best kept as an occasional snack.

descriptions.name: jus concentre
descriptions.description_en: Juice boiled down to concentrate its sugars, then used to sweeten products while keeping a natural-sounding label. The fibre is gone and the sugar behaves like added sugar.

descriptions.name: jus de fruits frais
descriptions.description_en: Freshly pressed fruit and vegetable juice. It keeps the vitamins and antioxidants but loses most of the fibre, so whole fruit remains preferable for blood sugar.

descriptions.name: jus de pommes concentre
descriptions.description_en: Concentrated apple juice, one of the most common "natural" sweeteners in industrial food. Nutritionally it is close to added sugar, with the fibre and most vitamins removed.

descriptions.name: jus de raisin concentre
descriptions.description_en: Concentrated grape juice used to sweeten products without declaring added sugar. It is rich in fructose and behaves metabolically much like a syrup.

descriptions.name: kefir
descriptions.description_en: Kefir, skyr, lassi and Greek yoghurt. Fermented dairy with live cultures and a high protein content; kefir carries a broader range of bacteria and yeasts than yoghurt.

descriptions.name: keratine
descriptions.description_en: The structural protein of hair, added to products to smooth and coat the strand. The protein itself is harmless, but some professional keratin straightening treatments release formaldehyde when heated.

descriptions.name: l-cysteine
descriptions.description_en: An amino acid (E920) used as a dough conditioner to speed up industrial bread making. Modern production is by bacterial fermentation, though it was historically extracted from feathers and hair.

descriptions.name: l-theanine
descriptions.description_en: An amino acid found almost exclusively in tea. It promotes calm alertness and offsets the jitteriness of caffeine, which is why tea feels different from coffee.

descriptions.name: lactate de calcium
descriptions.description_en: A firming agent and acidity regulator (E327) that also supplies calcium. It is well tolerated and one of the more benign mineral salts used in food.

descriptions.name: lactate de potassium
descriptions.description_en: A preservative and acidity regulator (E326) often used to reduce sodium in processed meat. It is considered safe, though people with kidney disease should limit added potassium salts.

descriptions.name: lactate de sodium
descriptions.description_en: The sodium salt of lactic acid (E325), used to preserve and retain moisture in meat and baked goods. It is well tolerated but adds sodium to an already salty product category.

descriptions.name: lactitol
descriptions.description_en: A polyol (E966) derived from lactose, poorly absorbed and used in sugar-free products. It reaches the colon largely intact, which is why it carries a laxative warning above 10%.

descriptions.name: lait
descriptions.description_en: Whole milk, a natural source of complete protein, calcium, iodine and B12. Well tolerated by most, apart from those with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

descriptions.name: lait de chevre
descriptions.description_en: Goat, sheep and buffalo milk, plus raw milk and buttermilk. Their fat globules are smaller than cow's milk, which many people find easier to digest.

descriptions.name: lait ecreme
descriptions.description_en: Skimmed milk, keeping the protein, calcium and B vitamins while removing the fat. It also loses the fat-soluble vitamins A and D unless they are added back.

descriptions.name: lait en poudre
descriptions.description_en: Milk dried at high temperature for shelf life. It keeps most nutrients, though heat processing can oxidise some cholesterol and degrade certain vitamins compared with fresh milk.

descriptions.name: lanoline
descriptions.description_en: A wax from sheep's wool that is highly effective at sealing moisture into dry skin and lips. Purified grades are safe, but it is a known contact allergen and lower grades can carry pesticide residues.

descriptions.name: lentilles
descriptions.description_en: Lentils, rich in plant protein, iron, folate and fibre. They have a low glycemic index, and pairing them with vitamin C improves absorption of their iron.

descriptions.name: levain
descriptions.description_en: Natural sourdough starter and traditional flatbreads. Long fermentation breaks down part of the gluten and phytates, making bread more digestible and its minerals more available.

descriptions.name: levure
descriptions.description_en: Baker's yeast, a living micro-organism that raises dough naturally. It also brings B vitamins and protein, and requires no chemical raising agents.

descriptions.name: lilial
descriptions.description_en: A synthetic floral fragrance (butylphenyl methylpropional) banned in EU cosmetics since March 2022. It was classified toxic to reproduction (CMR 1B) after animal studies showed effects on fertility and foetal development, and it is also a contact allergen.

descriptions.name: luteine
descriptions.description_en: A yellow carotenoid (E161b) from marigold and leafy greens. It concentrates in the retina and is associated with eye health, making it a colouring with real nutritional value.

descriptions.name: lycopene
