descriptions.description_en: The red pigment of tomatoes (E160d), one of the most studied dietary antioxidants. Used as a colouring, it retains its antioxidant properties.

descriptions.name: magnesium carbonates
descriptions.description_en: Refined magnesium salts used to prevent clumping, regulate acidity, or improve powder flow. Health: Large magnesium doses can cause diarrhea and abdominal cramping; food-additive quantities are usually much lower.

descriptions.name: magnesium chloride
descriptions.description_en: A refined magnesium salt used in tofu, mineral fortification, and texture control. Health: Large amounts may cause diarrhea, nausea, or abdominal cramping, especially in people with reduced kidney function.

descriptions.name: magnesium hydroxide
descriptions.description_en: A refined magnesium compound used to regulate acidity. At larger medicinal doses it also acts as a laxative. Health: Too much can cause diarrhea, cramping, and magnesium accumulation in people with kidney impairment.

descriptions.name: magnesium oxide
descriptions.description_en: A refined magnesium compound used to prevent clumping or regulate acidity. Health: Large doses may cause diarrhea or magnesium accumulation, particularly in people with impaired kidney function.

descriptions.name: magnesium silicate
descriptions.description_en: A processed mineral used to keep powders dry and free-flowing. The available modern data are limited for a complete long-term assessment. Health: Use should remain controlled because chronic exposure has not been characterized as thoroughly as for better-studied additives.

descriptions.name: magnesium trisilicate
descriptions.description_en: A mineral anti-caking compound used in powdered foods. Its long-term safety database is incomplete. Health: The concern is uncertainty from limited chronic and reproductive data, rather than confirmed toxicity from normal food use.

descriptions.name: mais déshydraté
descriptions.description_en: Dried or whole corn, a whole grain when the kernel is intact. It supplies fibre, B vitamins and carotenoids — quite different from the refined corn starch used in industrial food.

descriptions.name: maltitol
descriptions.description_en: A polyol (E965) widely used in sugar-free chocolate. It still raises blood sugar noticeably — more than other polyols — and is one of the most likely to cause bloating and laxative effects.

descriptions.name: maltodextrine
descriptions.description_en: An ultra-processed carbohydrate made by industrial hydrolysis of starch, often from corn. Its glycemic index reaches around 110, higher than table sugar, and studies link it to disrupted gut bacteria.

descriptions.name: mangue
descriptions.description_en: Tropical fruits such as mango, pineapple, papaya and passion fruit. They are dense in vitamins A and C and digestive enzymes, and their fibre balances their natural sugar.

descriptions.name: mannitol
descriptions.description_en: A polyol sweetener and anti-caking agent (E421) with roughly half the calories of sugar. Like all polyols it is poorly absorbed and carries a mandatory laxative warning above 10%.

descriptions.name: Mélamine
descriptions.description_en: An industrial resin chemical with no place in food. It was illegally added to milk products to fake protein readings, causing kidney failure in infants in 2008. IARC classifies it Group 2B, possibly carcinogenic.

descriptions.name: Mélamine (vaisselle)
descriptions.description_en: A resin used in unbreakable tableware. It is stable at normal temperatures but can migrate into food when heated, which is why melamine dishes should never go in a microwave or hold very hot food.

descriptions.name: menthol
descriptions.description_en: A cooling compound from mint, used in balms, toothpaste and scalp products. The cooling sensation is not an active benefit, and at higher concentrations it irritates skin and mucous membranes.

descriptions.name: mercure
descriptions.description_en: A heavy metal that is strongly neurotoxic, especially for the developing brain. Banned in EU cosmetics and tightly capped in fish and seafood. It accumulates in the body and is never safe at any deliberate dose.

descriptions.name: Mercure / Thimérosal
descriptions.description_en: Mercury and its preservative form thimerosal. Mercury is a potent neurotoxin that accumulates in the nervous system and kidneys; it is banned in EU cosmetics and strictly limited in food.

descriptions.name: metabisulfite de potassium
descriptions.description_en: A sulfite preservative (E224) common in winemaking and dried fruit. It must be declared as an allergen above 10 mg/kg and can cause asthma symptoms in sensitive people.

descriptions.name: metabisulfite de sodium
descriptions.description_en: One of the most widely used sulfites (E223), found in wine, dried fruit and seafood. It destroys some thiamine (vitamin B1) and is a declarable allergen above 10 mg/kg in the EU.

descriptions.name: methyl paraben
descriptions.description_en: A synthetic preservative used against molds and bacteria. It has weak biological activity in laboratory testing, but food use is regulated under a combined acceptable daily intake with ethyl paraben. Health: The practical concern is cumulative exposure from food, medicines, and personal-care products, not proven cancer from permitted food levels.

descriptions.name: methylcellulose
descriptions.description_en: A chemically modified cellulose (E461) used to thicken and bind, notably in plant-based meat substitutes. It is not absorbed and passes through as fibre, but it is a laboratory-modified ingredient.

descriptions.name: methylparaben
descriptions.description_en: A preservative (E218/E219) still permitted in limited EU food uses and widely used in cosmetics. It is the least potent paraben, though the family as a whole is under scrutiny for endocrine activity.

descriptions.name: Mica contaminé
descriptions.description_en: A mineral that gives cosmetics their shimmer. Natural mica can carry heavy metal impurities, and much of the global supply is linked to child labour in unregulated mines.

descriptions.name: Microplastiques / Microbilles
descriptions.description_en: Tiny plastic particles added to scrubs, toothpaste and cosmetics. The EU began banning intentionally added microplastics in 2023 because they pass through water treatment and accumulate in the environment.

descriptions.name: miel
descriptions.description_en: Honey, an unrefined sweetener carrying enzymes, antioxidants and antibacterial compounds. It is still mostly sugar, so it is a better sweetener rather than a free one — and never for infants under one.

descriptions.name: mixed acetic and tartaric acid esters of mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids
descriptions.description_en: A complex emulsifier made by chemically esterifying mono- and diglycerides. It improves dough performance, volume, and shelf stability in industrial foods. Health: No carcinogenic classification applies. Purity, total tartaric-acid exposure, and frequent consumption of heavily formulated foods are the main considerations.

descriptions.name: moah
descriptions.description_en: Mineral oil aromatic hydrocarbons, contaminants from packaging inks, machine lubricants and processing aids. EFSA considers those with three or more aromatic rings genotoxic and carcinogenic, and found their presence in infant formula to be of health concern.

descriptions.name: modified whey
descriptions.description_en: Whey that has been chemically or enzymatically altered for texture and shelf life. It is far removed from the original dairy ingredient and is characteristic of ultra-processed formulation.

descriptions.name: monk fruit
descriptions.description_en: Monk fruit (luo han guo) extract, a calorie-free sweetener from a Chinese fruit, sweetened by mogrosides rather than sugar. It does not raise blood glucose.

descriptions.name: mortadelle
descriptions.description_en: An emulsified, cured pork sausage. As a processed meat it falls under the IARC Group 1 classification, with regular consumption linked to a higher colorectal cancer risk.

descriptions.name: mosh
descriptions.description_en: Mineral oil saturated hydrocarbons, which migrate into food from packaging and machinery. EFSA concluded in 2023 that current dietary exposure raises no health concern, though they accumulate in the liver and lymphatic tissue and long-term effects remain uncertain.

descriptions.name: msg
descriptions.description_en: Monosodium glutamate (E621), a flavour enhancer that makes processed food taste richer. Regulators consider it safe at normal intake, but it is a reliable marker of ultra-processed food and can encourage overeating.

descriptions.name: mure
descriptions.description_en: Dark berries including blackberries, blackcurrants, cranberries and goji. Their deep colour comes from anthocyanins, plant compounds linked to cardiovascular and cognitive benefits.

descriptions.name: natamycine
descriptions.description_en: An antifungal (E235) applied to the surface of cheese and cured sausage. It is not absorbed through the gut wall, but it is an antibiotic-class compound, raising questions about resistance.

descriptions.name: neohesperidine dc
descriptions.description_en: A synthetic sweetener (E959) derived from bitter orange peel, several hundred times sweeter than sugar. It is authorised in the EU but not in the United States, and is used mainly to mask bitterness in industrial products.

descriptions.name: neotame
descriptions.description_en: An artificial sweetener (E961) built from aspartame, up to 13,000 times sweeter than sugar. EFSA re-evaluated it in 2025 and found no safety concern at permitted levels, though the WHO advises against sweeteners for weight control.

descriptions.name: niacinamide
descriptions.description_en: Vitamin B3 in its added form, used to fortify flours, cereals and drinks. The vitamin itself is beneficial and well tolerated; its presence mainly signals a refined product whose nutrients were added back after processing.

descriptions.name: nisine
descriptions.description_en: A natural antibacterial peptide (E234) produced by lactic bacteria, used in cheese and canned foods. It is digested like any protein and is one of the most benign preservatives available.

descriptions.name: nitrate de potassium
descriptions.description_en: A curing salt (E252) used in charcuterie and cheese. In the body it converts to nitrite and forms nitrosamines: IARC classifies ingested nitrate under conditions leading to nitrosation as Group 2A, probably carcinogenic.

descriptions.name: nitrite de potassium
descriptions.description_en: A curing agent (E249) that fixes the pink colour of cured meats and blocks botulism. It forms nitrosamines during curing and cooking; IARC rates ingested nitrite leading to nitrosation as Group 2A, probably carcinogenic.

descriptions.name: nitrite de sodium
descriptions.description_en: A curing agent (E250) that fixes the pink colour of cured meat and blocks botulism. During curing and cooking it forms nitrosamines; IARC rates ingested nitrite leading to nitrosation as Group 2A, probably carcinogenic.

descriptions.name: nitrosamine
descriptions.description_en: Compounds formed when nitrites react with proteins in cured meat or under high-heat cooking. Several nitrosamines, including NDMA, are rated IARC Group 2A and are a main reason processed meat is classified Group 1.

descriptions.name: Noir de carbone
descriptions.description_en: Carbon black, a pigment used in cosmetics, inks and tyres. IARC classifies it Group 2B, possibly carcinogenic, based on inhalation exposure; the risk in finished cosmetics is far lower.

descriptions.name: noisette
descriptions.description_en: Hazelnuts, high in vitamin E, monounsaturated fat and manganese. Pure hazelnut paste is a genuinely nutritious ingredient, unlike the sweetened spreads it usually ends up in.

descriptions.name: noix
descriptions.description_en: Walnuts, cashews and pistachios. Walnuts stand out as one of the few plant sources of omega-3 ALA, and all provide protein, fibre and minerals in a whole-food form.

descriptions.name: noix de coco
descriptions.description_en: Coconut in its whole forms — flesh, milk, cream and water. It is high in saturated fat, mostly medium-chain, so it is nutritious but best used with a degree of moderation.

descriptions.name: Nonylphénols éthoxylés (NPE)
descriptions.description_en: Detergent surfactants that degrade into nonylphenol, an endocrine disruptor and a priority hazardous substance in EU water law. Their use in consumer products is heavily restricted in Europe.

descriptions.name: octinoxate
descriptions.description_en: A chemical UV filter (with homosalate and octisalate) that penetrates the skin and is detectable in blood. EU scientific committees have cut the permitted levels over endocrine-disruption concerns, and some regions restrict it to protect coral reefs.

descriptions.name: oeuf
descriptions.description_en: Eggs, one of the most complete foods available: high-quality protein, choline, vitamin D, B12 and lutein. Dietary cholesterol has been cleared of the concerns once attached to it.

descriptions.name: okra
descriptions.description_en: Okra, bamboo shoots, bean sprouts and lotus root. Okra's soluble fibre helps regulate blood sugar and cholesterol, and all are low-calorie whole vegetables.

descriptions.name: onion
descriptions.description_en: A whole vegetable rich in quercetin and prebiotic fibre that feeds beneficial gut bacteria. It adds depth of flavour without salt or sugar, whether fresh or dehydrated.

descriptions.name: or
descriptions.description_en: Gold leaf (E175) used to decorate confectionery and drinks. It passes through the body unabsorbed, but EFSA could not complete its safety re-evaluation for lack of data on nanoparticle content.

descriptions.name: orange
descriptions.description_en: Citrus fruits rich in vitamin C, fibre and flavonoids. Eaten whole rather than juiced, they support immunity and iron absorption without the sugar spike of juice.

descriptions.name: orange b
descriptions.description_en: A synthetic dye whose only remaining approved use in the US is colouring hot dog and sausage casings. It has never been authorised in the European Union.

descriptions.name: orge
descriptions.description_en: Barley, exceptionally high in beta-glucan fibre. It has one of the lowest glycemic responses of any grain and supports both cholesterol control and gut health.

descriptions.name: oxidized starch
descriptions.description_en: Starch chemically modified to improve thickening, stability, and processing performance. It is used to engineer consistent texture in sauces, fillings, and processed foods. Health: No specific major toxicity is established at authorized levels. It is primarily a marker of industrial formulation.

descriptions.name: oxybenzone
descriptions.description_en: A chemical UV filter absorbed through the skin and repeatedly flagged for hormonal activity. Its permitted concentration has been reduced in the EU, and it is banned in Hawaii and Palau for coral reef damage.

descriptions.name: oxyde d ethylene
descriptions.description_en: A fumigant banned in EU food production and classified as mutagenic, carcinogenic and reprotoxic, with no safe level established. Its detection in imported sesame and locust bean gum triggered the largest food recall operation in EU history from 2020.

descriptions.name: oxydes de fer
descriptions.description_en: Mineral pigments (E172) used to colour coatings, sweets and cosmetics. They pass through the body largely unabsorbed and EFSA considers them safe, but they add no nutritional value.

descriptions.name: oxygen
descriptions.description_en: A natural gas used in controlled-atmosphere packaging and processing. Health: It is not toxic at food-packaging exposure. It can accelerate oxidation, rancidity, and vitamin loss in some foods.

descriptions.name: pain blanc
descriptions.description_en: Bread made from refined flour, with the bran and germ removed. It raises blood sugar quickly and delivers little fibre; wholemeal or sourdough versions are substantially better.

descriptions.name: pain complet
descriptions.description_en: Wholemeal, rye and multigrain breads made with the whole grain. They deliver several times the fibre of white bread, with a gentler effect on blood sugar.

descriptions.name: palmitate d ascorbyle
descriptions.description_en: A fat-soluble form of vitamin C (E304) used to keep oils from going rancid. It is broken down into vitamin C and palmitic acid in the body, and is considered safe at permitted levels.

descriptions.name: pantothenate de calcium
descriptions.description_en: Vitamin B5 in its added form, used to enrich foods, drinks and supplements. Harmless and genuinely useful, but it usually appears in products that lost their natural nutrients during refining.

descriptions.name: paprika extract, capsanthin and capsorubin
descriptions.description_en: A concentrated red-orange color extracted from paprika and processed to standardize pigment strength. It is not considered a high-risk additive at permitted levels. Health: Quality control is important for solvent residues and purity. Rare paprika-related allergic reactions may occur in sensitive people.

descriptions.name: Parabènes (méthyl, éthyl, propyl, butyl)
descriptions.description_en: A family of preservatives with weak oestrogen-like activity. Methyl and ethyl parabens remain permitted at low levels in the EU, while propyl and butyl are capped and isopropyl and isobutyl forms are banned.

descriptions.name: paraffinum liquidum
descriptions.description_en: Liquid petroleum oil used as an emollient in cosmetics. Untreated and mildly treated mineral oils are IARC Group 1 human carcinogens; pharmaceutical-grade refining lowers the risk but MOAH residues remain a concern.

descriptions.name: paraquat
descriptions.description_en: A herbicide banned in the EU since 2007 because of its extreme acute toxicity — a small ingested dose can be fatal with no antidote. Epidemiological studies also associate exposure with a raised risk of Parkinson's disease.

descriptions.name: pastrami
descriptions.description_en: Brined, smoked and spiced beef. It falls under processed meat, an IARC Group 1 human carcinogen, and carries a heavy salt load. Regular intake is linked to colorectal cancer.

descriptions.name: pate de cacao
descriptions.description_en: Cocoa mass, the ground whole cocoa bean before sugar is added. It keeps all the flavanols, fibre and minerals of the bean and is the base of real dark chocolate.

descriptions.name: patent blue v
descriptions.description_en: A synthetic blue dye used only to change appearance and provide no nutritional value. Current authorized uses have not been shown to create a general safety concern, but rare hypersensitivity reactions are possible. Health: People with a history of reactions to synthetic dyes should be cautious. The additive mainly signals a highly formulated product.

descriptions.name: pates completes
descriptions.description_en: Whole wheat pasta, soba, udon and rice noodles. Whole grain versions keep their fibre and minerals, and pasta cooked al dente has a lower glycemic response.

descriptions.name: pcb
descriptions.description_en: Polychlorinated biphenyls, banned industrial oils that persist for decades in the environment and concentrate in fatty fish. IARC classifies them Group 1 human carcinogens, and they are also linked to hormonal and developmental effects.

descriptions.name: peche
descriptions.description_en: Stone fruits such as peaches, apricots, plums and cherries. They provide fibre, potassium and carotenoids, and cherries in particular carry anti-inflammatory compounds.

descriptions.name: pectine
descriptions.description_en: A soluble fibre (E440) extracted from apples and citrus peel, used to set jams. It is a natural fruit fibre that also helps lower cholesterol.

descriptions.name: peg-
descriptions.description_en: PEG compounds and sodium laureth sulfate, made by ethoxylation. The process can leave traces of 1,4-dioxane, a possible carcinogen, and PEGs increase how much the skin absorbs other ingredients.

descriptions.name: pepperoni
descriptions.description_en: A cured, fermented pork and beef sausage preserved with nitrites. It is a processed meat, high in sodium and saturated fat, and regular intake is linked to colorectal cancer risk.

descriptions.name: peptides
descriptions.description_en: Short chains of amino acids used to signal repair processes in the skin. They are well tolerated and non-irritating, though results vary widely depending on the specific peptide and formulation.

descriptions.name: Perchloréthylène
descriptions.description_en: The classic dry-cleaning solvent. IARC classifies it Group 2A, probably carcinogenic to humans, and it is being phased out or tightly controlled in many countries because it lingers on treated fabrics.

descriptions.name: peroxyde de benzoyle
descriptions.description_en: An effective antibacterial acne treatment that kills the bacteria driving breakouts. It is drying and irritating at higher strengths, and it permanently bleaches fabric and hair on contact.

descriptions.name: petits pois
descriptions.description_en: Peas, beans and lentils in all their varieties. Pulses combine plant protein, fibre and slow carbohydrates, and regular intake is associated with better blood sugar and cholesterol.

descriptions.name: PFAS / PFC dans textiles
descriptions.description_en: Water- and stain-repellent "forever chemicals" applied to textiles and packaging. PFOA was classified IARC Group 1 human carcinogen in 2023; PFAS accumulate in the body and do not break down in the environment.

descriptions.name: PFOA / PTFE (Teflon)
descriptions.description_en: Non-stick coating and the chemicals used to make it. PTFE itself is inert, but PFOA — historically used in its manufacture — was classified an IARC Group 1 carcinogen in 2023. Scratched or overheated pans are the real concern.

descriptions.name: pgpr
descriptions.description_en: Polyglycerol polyricinoleate (E476), a synthetic emulsifier from castor oil used to cut cocoa butter costs in chocolate. Authorised in the EU, it signals a cheaper, more industrial formulation.

descriptions.name: phenoxyethanol
descriptions.description_en: A widely used preservative, permitted in the EU up to 1% in cosmetics. It is generally well tolerated, though France's health agency advised against using it on the nappy area of children under three.

descriptions.name: phosphate de calcium
descriptions.description_en: A phosphate salt (E341) used as an anti-caking agent and firming agent, and to fortify foods with calcium. It falls under EFSA's combined phosphate limit, which many diets already approach.

descriptions.name: phosphate de diamidon
descriptions.description_en: Distarch phosphate (E1412), a cross-linked modified starch used to hold texture through heating and freezing. Safe by EFSA standards, but purely technical and typical of ultra-processed products.

descriptions.name: phosphate de diamidon acetyle
descriptions.description_en: Acetylated distarch phosphate (E1422), a doubly modified starch used in sauces, ready meals and desserts. It adds texture and shelf life but no nutritional value, and marks a highly industrial recipe.

descriptions.name: phosphate de diamidon acetyle e1414
descriptions.description_en: A doubly modified starch (E1414) built to survive heating, freezing and acidity. It adds texture and shelf life without nutrition, and signals an industrially engineered recipe.

descriptions.name: phosphate de diamidon hydroxypropyle
descriptions.description_en: One of the most common modified starches (E1442), used in sauces, desserts and ready meals. Regarded as safe by EFSA, but a clear technical marker of ultra-processed food.

descriptions.name: phosphate de monoamidon
descriptions.description_en: A modified starch (E1410) used to thicken and stabilise processed food. EFSA considers modified starches safe, but they are refined carbohydrates and a marker of ultra-processing.

descriptions.name: phosphate de potassium
descriptions.description_en: A phosphate salt (E340) used as a buffer and stabiliser. EFSA set a combined limit for all phosphate additives; people with reduced kidney function should keep added phosphates low.

descriptions.name: phosphate de sodium
descriptions.description_en: An added phosphate (E339) used to bind water and hold texture. Added phosphates are absorbed far more readily than natural ones, and EFSA has flagged high total intake as a concern for kidney and heart health.

descriptions.name: phosphated distarch phosphate
descriptions.description_en: A cross-linked and phosphorylated starch designed to resist heat, acid, and mechanical processing. Health: It has no established carcinogenic classification. Its role is technological rather than nutritional.

descriptions.name: Phosphates (détergents)
descriptions.description_en: Phosphates in detergents soften water and boost cleaning, but they drive algal blooms that suffocate rivers and lakes. The EU has restricted them in household laundry and dishwasher products.

descriptions.name: phosphatides d ammonium
descriptions.description_en: An emulsifier (E442) used almost exclusively in chocolate to control flow during moulding. It is authorised at low levels but is a synthetic phosphate derivative with no place in traditional chocolate.

descriptions.name: phtalate
descriptions.description_en: Plasticisers that soften plastics and fix fragrances. Several are classified as toxic to reproduction and act as endocrine disruptors; the most harmful are banned or authorisation-restricted in the EU.

descriptions.name: Phtalate DBP
descriptions.description_en: Dibutyl phthalate, once common in nail polish. It is classified as toxic to reproduction in the EU, banned from cosmetics, and on the REACH authorisation list because of its endocrine effects.

descriptions.name: Phtalate DEHP
descriptions.description_en: The most widely used plasticiser in soft PVC. It is classified as toxic to reproduction in the EU, banned in cosmetics and in toys, and restricted in food-contact and medical plastics.

descriptions.name: Phtalate DEP
descriptions.description_en: Diethyl phthalate, the phthalate most used to fix fragrances. It is considered less toxic than DEHP or DBP and is still permitted in the EU, but it is absorbed through skin and detected in most people.

descriptions.name: Phtalates (parfums)
descriptions.description_en: Phthalates hidden inside the generic word "fragrance", where they make scent last longer. Because the label discloses nothing, the consumer cannot tell which phthalate is present or at what level.

descriptions.name: plantain
descriptions.description_en: Plantain, tamarind and physalis. Plantain is a starchy staple rich in resistant starch and potassium, best cooked, and a whole food in every sense.

descriptions.name: plomb
descriptions.description_en: A heavy metal with no safe level of exposure according to the WHO. It is strongly neurotoxic — particularly damaging to children's brain development — and banned in EU cosmetics. Inorganic lead compounds are rated IARC Group 2A.

descriptions.name: Plomb (acétate de plomb)
descriptions.description_en: Lead acetate, once used in hair dyes and cosmetics. Lead is neurotoxic with no safe exposure level per the WHO, damaging brain development in children. It is banned in cosmetics in the EU and the US.

descriptions.name: poireau
descriptions.description_en: Leeks, spring onions, chives and wild garlic. They provide prebiotic fibre that feeds beneficial gut bacteria, along with sulphur compounds with antibacterial activity.

descriptions.name: pois chiches
descriptions.description_en: Chickpeas, a pulse combining protein, fibre and slow carbohydrates. They are filling, support stable blood sugar, and form the base of traditional dishes like hummus.

descriptions.name: poivre
descriptions.description_en: Pepper, paprika, cumin, oregano, basil, thyme and rosemary. Culinary spices and herbs are among the most antioxidant-dense foods by weight, and they replace salt as a flavour source.

descriptions.name: Polycarbonate (plastique #7)
descriptions.description_en: A hard, clear plastic made from bisphenol A. BPA leaches out with heat, scratches and age — a real concern now that the EU has banned BPA in food contact materials.

descriptions.name: polydextrose
descriptions.description_en: A synthetic soluble fibre (E1200) made from glucose, used to add bulk and fibre while cutting sugar. It is largely unabsorbed and acts as a prebiotic, but large amounts cause bloating.

descriptions.name: polyphosphate
descriptions.description_en: Polyphosphates (E452) used to bind water, emulsify and stabilise processed meat and cheese. They count toward EFSA's combined phosphate limit and are a clear marker of industrial processing.

descriptions.name: polysorbate 20
descriptions.description_en: A synthetic emulsifier (E432) derived from sorbitol and ethylene oxide. Authorised at limited levels, but emulsifiers of this family have been linked in studies to disruption of the gut barrier.

descriptions.name: polysorbate 40
descriptions.description_en: A synthetic emulsifier (E434) used to blend fats and water in industrial food. Permitted at capped levels; animal studies on polysorbates suggest effects on gut bacteria and inflammation.

descriptions.name: polysorbate 60
descriptions.description_en: A synthetic emulsifier (E435) common in whipped toppings and baked goods. It is authorised but purely technical, and its family has been tied to gut microbiome changes in research.

descriptions.name: polysorbate 65
descriptions.description_en: A synthetic emulsifier (E436) used in ice cream and frozen desserts to control texture. Regulated at low levels, it is a clear marker of an industrially engineered product.

descriptions.name: polysorbate 80
descriptions.description_en: A synthetic emulsifier (E433) widely used in ice cream, sauces and dressings. Animal and cell studies link polysorbate 80 to thinning of the protective gut mucus layer and low-grade inflammation.

descriptions.name: Polystyrène (plastique #6)
descriptions.description_en: The plastic of foam trays and disposable cups. Its building block styrene is classified IARC Group 2A, probably carcinogenic, and migration increases with hot or fatty foods.

descriptions.name: polyvinyl alcohol (pva)
descriptions.description_en: A synthetic polymer used in edible films, coatings, and supplement capsules. It is only partly absorbed and is used for a technological purpose. Health: The principal concern is product purity and residual manufacturing chemicals rather than a proven toxic effect at permitted levels.

descriptions.name: polyvinylpolypyrrolidone (pvpp)
descriptions.description_en: A synthetic, insoluble polymer used to clarify beverages or stabilize supplements. It is poorly absorbed from the digestive tract. Health: Safety depends on strict limits for residual monomers and manufacturing impurities.

descriptions.name: pomme
descriptions.description_en: Apples, pears, bananas and lemons — whole fruit eaten as it grows. Their fibre slows sugar absorption, and their vitamins and polyphenols come packaged exactly as the body handles best.

descriptions.name: pomme de terre
descriptions.description_en: Potatoes, sweet potatoes and root vegetables. Nutritious whole foods rich in potassium and fibre — how they are cooked matters far more than the vegetable itself.

descriptions.name: ponceau 4r
descriptions.description_en: Cochineal Red A (E124), a synthetic azo dye subject to the EU warning label on children's activity and attention. It is banned from food in the United States, Norway and Finland.

descriptions.name: potassium aluminum silicate
descriptions.description_en: An aluminum-containing mineral used to improve powder flow. It adds to aluminum exposure and has limited modern toxicology data. Health: Frequent intake from several aluminum-containing foods may increase total exposure, especially for vulnerable consumers.

descriptions.name: potassium aluminum sulfate
descriptions.description_en: Also called potassium alum, this compound is used as a firming or processing agent and adds aluminum to the diet. Health: Long-term concern relates to cumulative aluminum exposure, not an immediate poisoning effect from a single serving.

descriptions.name: potassium carbonates
descriptions.description_en: Refined mineral salts used to control acidity, improve dough, or support manufacturing. They are not considered harmful at normal food levels. Health: Very high potassium intake can be dangerous for people with kidney disease or those taking medicines that raise blood potassium.

descriptions.name: potassium chloride
descriptions.description_en: A refined mineral salt used to replace sodium, control flavor, or support texture. Health: Excess potassium can cause dangerous heart-rhythm problems in people with kidney disease or certain medications. Normal consumers usually tolerate food amounts.

descriptions.name: potassium ferrocyanide
descriptions.description_en: A stable anti-caking complex used mainly in salt. It does not normally release dangerous free cyanide during ordinary food use. Health: The additive should still remain within regulatory limits and purity specifications.

descriptions.name: potassium gluconate
descriptions.description_en: A potassium salt used for mineral fortification and product stability. Health: Excess potassium can be dangerous for people with kidney disease or medicines that impair potassium removal.

descriptions.name: potassium hydroxide
descriptions.description_en: A strong alkali used to adjust pH or manufacture other ingredients. It is neutralized or highly diluted during food processing. Health: The raw chemical can cause severe burns, but properly controlled food use should not retain this corrosive effect.

descriptions.name: potassium sulfates
descriptions.description_en: Refined potassium salts used to regulate acidity or support processing. Health: People with kidney disease must avoid excessive potassium because it can disturb heart rhythm.

descriptions.name: poudre a lever
descriptions.description_en: Baking powder, a blend of a carbonate and an acid salt that makes dough rise. It is harmless in itself, though some formulations use aluminium-based acids that add to total aluminium intake.

descriptions.name: céleri
descriptions.description_en: Celery, celeriac, fennel, asparagus and artichoke. Low in calories and high in fibre and potassium, with artichoke and asparagus also acting as prebiotics.

descriptions.name: poulet
descriptions.description_en: Chicken, turkey and other poultry. Lean, high in complete protein and B vitamins, and among the lightest animal proteins when the skin is removed.

descriptions.name: ppd
descriptions.description_en: Para-phenylenediamine, the base of most permanent dark hair dyes. A strong skin sensitiser that can trigger severe allergic reactions; it is capped in the EU and illegal in "black henna" temporary tattoos.

descriptions.name: propionate de calcium
descriptions.description_en: A mould inhibitor (E282) used mainly in industrial bread. It is considered safe by EFSA and occurs naturally in some cheeses, though its presence signals bread built for long shelf life.

descriptions.name: propionate de potassium
descriptions.description_en: A mould inhibitor (E283) used in packaged bread and baked goods. Considered safe by EFSA, though it is only needed when bread must last far beyond its natural life.

descriptions.name: propionate de sodium
descriptions.description_en: A bread preservative (E281) that blocks mould and rope spoilage. EFSA considers it safe at permitted levels; it marks industrial rather than fresh-baked bread.

descriptions.name: propyl paraben
descriptions.description_en: A paraben preservative that is no longer authorized as a food additive in the European Union. Regulators could not establish an acceptable daily intake from the available reproductive-toxicity data. Health: The unresolved concern involves possible reproductive effects at sufficient exposure. Non-authorization does not prove that ordinary trace exposure causes cancer.

descriptions.name: Propylène glycol
descriptions.description_en: A synthetic solvent and moisture-retaining agent used in flavors, colors, enzymes, and processed foods. It is not the same substance as toxic ethylene glycol. Health: Very high exposure can cause hyperosmolality, lactic acidosis, nervous-system depression, and kidney stress, especially in infants or people with impaired liver or kidney function.

descriptions.name: propylparaben
descriptions.description_en: A preservative removed from the EU list of permitted food additives over endocrine-disruption concerns, and restricted in cosmetics. It mimics oestrogen in laboratory studies and is banned from food in California from 2027.

descriptions.name: proteine de feve
descriptions.description_en: Protein extracted from fava beans, used to boost protein content in plant-based products. Nutritionally useful, though an isolate rather than a whole food.

descriptions.name: proteine de pois
descriptions.description_en: Protein isolated from yellow peas by industrial extraction. It is a useful plant protein, but stripped of the fibre and micronutrients of the whole pulse.

descriptions.name: proteine de soja
descriptions.description_en: Soy protein isolated through industrial processing, often with hexane solvent. It is frequently GM-derived outside the EU and is used to bulk up protein content in reconstituted foods.

descriptions.name: proteines hydrolysees
descriptions.description_en: Proteins broken down with acid or enzymes, which releases free glutamate and acts as a hidden flavour enhancer. The process can also generate unwanted by-products such as chloropropanols.

descriptions.name: protoxyde d azote
descriptions.description_en: Nitrous oxide (E942), the propellant in aerosol whipped cream. It is inert in food use and leaves no residue, though inhaling it recreationally causes serious neurological harm.

descriptions.name: ptfe
descriptions.description_en: The non-stick coating on cookware. PTFE itself is not classified as carcinogenic, but PFOA — long used to manufacture it — is an IARC Group 1 human carcinogen. Overheated pans also release toxic fumes.

descriptions.name: pullulan
descriptions.description_en: A fermentation-produced carbohydrate polymer used to make edible films, capsules, and coatings. Health: Several grams at once may cause abdominal fullness, gas, bloating, or cramps in some people.

descriptions.name: PVC (plastique #3)
descriptions.description_en: A rigid plastic softened with phthalate plasticisers that migrate into fatty foods. Vinyl chloride, its building block, is a confirmed carcinogen, though it is largely bound in the finished material.

descriptions.name: pvp
descriptions.description_en: Polyvinylpyrrolidone (E1201), a synthetic polymer used to clarify drinks and coat tablets. It is not absorbed by the gut and is considered safe, serving a purely technical purpose.

descriptions.name: pyridoxine chlorhydrate
descriptions.description_en: Vitamin B6 in its added form, common in fortified foods and supplements. It is effective and safe at normal levels; very high long-term supplement doses are the only real concern.

descriptions.name: quaternium-15
descriptions.description_en: A formaldehyde-releasing preservative and one of the strongest emitters of the group. Formaldehyde is an IARC Group 1 human carcinogen; quaternium-15 is now prohibited in EU cosmetics.

descriptions.name: quinoa
descriptions.description_en: Quinoa, a seed rather than a true cereal, and one of the rare plant foods providing all nine essential amino acids. It is naturally gluten-free and rich in magnesium and iron.

descriptions.name: raisin
descriptions.description_en: Grapes, rich in polyphenols including resveratrol in the skin. Naturally higher in sugar than most fruit, but eaten whole the fibre keeps the response moderate.

descriptions.name: rebaudioside m
descriptions.description_en: A steviol glycoside with a cleaner taste than earlier stevia extracts, now often produced by fermentation rather than leaf extraction. It is approved and calorie-free, but industrially manufactured.

descriptions.name: Résorcinol
descriptions.description_en: A compound used in permanent hair dyes. It is a skin sensitiser and is flagged as a suspected endocrine disruptor affecting thyroid function; its level in cosmetics is capped in the EU.

descriptions.name: rhubarbe
descriptions.description_en: Rhubarb, quince and mirabelle plums — tart fruits low in sugar and high in fibre. Rhubarb leaves are toxic, but the stalks are perfectly safe and rich in vitamin K.

descriptions.name: riboflavine
descriptions.description_en: Vitamin B2 (E101), used as a yellow colouring. It is an essential nutrient with a genuine nutritional role, and one of the most benign colourings in use.

descriptions.name: ricotta
descriptions.description_en: Italian cheeses from ricotta and mozzarella to parmesan and gorgonzola. Traditionally made with few ingredients; ricotta is notably lower in fat and salt than aged varieties.

descriptions.name: riz
descriptions.description_en: Rice, a staple grain. Brown rice keeps the bran and its fibre, B vitamins and minerals; white rice loses most of them. Rice can carry inorganic arsenic, so varying grains is wise.

descriptions.name: riz basmati
descriptions.description_en: Basmati, jasmine, black, red and wild rice. Basmati has a notably lower glycemic index than most rice, and the pigmented varieties add antioxidants along with their fibre.

descriptions.name: riz précuit
descriptions.description_en: Rice pre-cooked and dried for speed. The processing costs some vitamins and raises the glycemic response compared with regular rice, though parboiled versions retain more nutrients.

descriptions.name: rouge 3
descriptions.description_en: Erythrosine (E127), a petroleum-based cherry-red dye. The FDA revoked its authorisation in food and ingested drugs in January 2025 after it caused cancer in male rats, with reformulation required by 2027.

descriptions.name: rouge 40
descriptions.description_en: Allura Red (E129), a petroleum-derived synthetic dye. EU law requires a warning label stating it may affect children's activity and attention, and the FDA is phasing it out of the US food supply.

descriptions.name: rouge de betterave
descriptions.description_en: Betanin (E162), the natural red pigment of beetroot. It is a plant extract with antioxidant activity, though it fades with heat and light, which limits its industrial use.

descriptions.name: saccharine
descriptions.description_en: One of the oldest artificial sweeteners (E954). Once suspected of causing bladder cancer in rats, it was later cleared for humans and delisted as a carcinogen, but remains a purely synthetic additive.

descriptions.name: salami
descriptions.description_en: A dry fermented and cured sausage. As a processed meat it falls under the IARC Group 1 classification: nitrite curing and fermentation generate compounds tied to colorectal cancer.

descriptions.name: salt
descriptions.description_en: Sodium chloride, essential for fluid balance and nerve function but present in excess in most processed food. High sodium intake raises blood pressure, and the WHO recommends staying under 5 g of salt a day.

descriptions.name: sarrasin
descriptions.description_en: Buckwheat, a gluten-free seed rich in rutin, magnesium and complete plant protein. Its low glycemic index makes it a good choice for stable blood sugar.

descriptions.name: saucisse
descriptions.description_en: Sausages, including hot dogs and merguez, are processed meats classified IARC Group 1 human carcinogens (2015). Regular intake raises colorectal cancer risk; they are also high in salt and saturated fat.

descriptions.name: saucisson
descriptions.description_en: A dry-cured sausage preserved with salt and nitrites. It falls under processed meat, an IARC Group 1 human carcinogen, with regular consumption linked to colorectal cancer.

descriptions.name: saumon sauvage
descriptions.description_en: Wild salmon, sardines, mackerel and anchovies. Small oily fish are the best dietary source of long-chain omega-3 EPA and DHA, with low mercury and high vitamin D.

descriptions.name: sel d aspartame-acesulfame
descriptions.description_en: A combined salt of aspartame and acesulfame K (E962), used to balance the aftertaste of each. It carries the concerns of both parent sweeteners, including aspartame's IARC Group 2B classification.

descriptions.name: sels d acides gras
descriptions.description_en: Fatty acid salts (E470), used as anti-caking and glazing agents rather than as a food fat. They are refined industrial derivatives typical of processed formulations.

descriptions.name: shellac
descriptions.description_en: A resin (E904) secreted by the lac insect, used to glaze sweets, coffee beans and tablets. It is not absorbed, but it is of insect origin and therefore not vegetarian.

descriptions.name: silicate alumino-calcique
descriptions.description_en: Calcium aluminosilicate (E556), an anti-caking agent that contributes to overall aluminium intake. EFSA has flagged dietary aluminium as a concern for accumulation in the body over time.

descriptions.name: silicate alumino-potassique
descriptions.description_en: Potassium aluminosilicate (E555), an anti-caking and glazing agent. Like other aluminium-based additives, it adds to total aluminium exposure, which EFSA considers should be kept low.

descriptions.name: silicate alumino-sodique
descriptions.description_en: Sodium aluminosilicate (E554), used to stop powders clumping. It contributes to dietary aluminium, which accumulates in the body and is why EFSA set a weekly tolerable intake.

descriptions.name: silicate de sodium
descriptions.description_en: Sodium silicate (E550), a technical anti-caking and preservation aid. It is strongly alkaline in concentrated form and serves purely industrial purposes, with no nutritional role.

descriptions.name: silice
descriptions.description_en: Silicon dioxide (E551), an anti-caking agent in powders and dried mixes. EFSA could not confirm the safety of its nanoparticle fraction in its re-evaluation and called for stricter specifications.

descriptions.name: silicon dioxide
descriptions.description_en: A finely divided mineral powder used to prevent clumping and improve flow in seasonings, powders, and supplements. Health: Current authorized food uses are not considered a general safety concern, but particle characterization and metal impurities require strict specifications.

descriptions.name: sirop de ble
descriptions.description_en: A syrup made by breaking down wheat starch into sugars. It is marketed as a natural sweetener but behaves like any glucose syrup, with a high glycemic impact and no nutrients.

descriptions.name: sirop de glucose
descriptions.description_en: A syrup produced by industrial hydrolysis of corn or wheat starch. It has a very high glycemic index, causes sharp blood-sugar spikes and brings no nutrients — a hallmark of ultra-processed food.

descriptions.name: sirop de glucose-fructose
descriptions.description_en: High-fructose corn syrup, a cheap industrial sweetener. Its fructose load is processed almost entirely by the liver and is linked to non-alcoholic fatty liver disease and metabolic syndrome.

descriptions.name: sirop de polyglycitol
descriptions.description_en: A polyol syrup (E964) made by hydrogenating starch, used as a bulk sweetener in sugar-free products. Like all polyols it is poorly absorbed and carries a mandatory laxative warning above 10%.

descriptions.name: sirop de riz
descriptions.description_en: Rice syrup, often sold as a healthier sweetener. It is almost pure glucose with a very high glycemic index, and rice-based products can carry inorganic arsenic residues.

descriptions.name: sirop de yacon
descriptions.description_en: Yacon and date syrups. Yacon is unusual in being rich in prebiotic fructo-oligosaccharides that are poorly absorbed, giving sweetness with a lower sugar impact.

descriptions.name: SLS (Sodium Lauryl Sulfate)
descriptions.description_en: A powerful foaming detergent used in shampoos, toothpaste and cleaners. It is not carcinogenic, but it is a well-documented irritant that strips skin and scalp with frequent use.

descriptions.name: sodium aluminum phosphate, acidic
descriptions.description_en: An acidic aluminum salt used in some baking powders and bakery products to control gas release. Health: It adds both aluminum and sodium. Heavy reliance on products containing aluminum additives can increase total exposure above recommended limits.

descriptions.name: sodium aluminum silicate
descriptions.description_en: An industrial anti-caking mineral that also contributes aluminum. The toxicology database has not supported a fully conclusive modern assessment. Health: Cumulative aluminum exposure and incomplete long-term data are the main reasons for concern.

descriptions.name: sodium aluminum sulfate
descriptions.description_en: An aluminum- and sodium-containing industrial salt used in some baking powders and processing applications. Health: It increases cumulative aluminum and sodium exposure. Frequent consumption of several aluminum-containing products is the main concern.

descriptions.name: sodium benzoate
descriptions.description_en: A preservative (E211) used in acidic drinks and sauces. Combined with vitamin C, and helped by heat or light, it can form traces of benzene — a reason to avoid drinks that list both.

descriptions.name: sodium ethyl paraben
descriptions.description_en: The water-soluble sodium form of ethyl paraben. It is an industrial antimicrobial preservative and contributes to the same combined paraben exposure limit as ethyl paraben. Health: The main concern is cumulative exposure to parabens rather than an immediate toxic effect at permitted levels.

descriptions.name: sodium ferrocyanide
descriptions.description_en: A stable iron-cyanide complex used in salt to prevent clumping. It is not the same as free cyanide under normal food conditions. Health: Current authorized uses are low. Purity and compliance with exposure limits are more relevant than the alarming chemical name.

descriptions.name: sodium gluconate
descriptions.description_en: A refined sodium salt used to bind metals, stabilize products, and control acidity. Health: Its main nutritional concern is added sodium rather than specific toxicity.

descriptions.name: sodium hydroxide
descriptions.description_en: A powerful alkaline processing agent used for pretzels, olives, cocoa, and pH control. It is consumed only after reaction, neutralization, washing, or dilution. Health: The concentrated chemical is corrosive. Correct processing must prevent caustic residues in the final food.

descriptions.name: sodium methyl paraben
descriptions.description_en: The sodium salt of methyl paraben, designed to dissolve more easily in water. It is a synthetic preservative counted within the same combined exposure limit as methyl and ethyl parabens. Health: Repeated exposure from several sources is more relevant than a single food serving.

descriptions.name: sodium propyl paraben
descriptions.description_en: The sodium form of propyl paraben, also no longer authorized as a food additive in the European Union. Its safety could not be adequately confirmed from the available reproductive-toxicity evidence. Health: Avoid as a declared food additive where it is not authorized. The concern is insufficient safety assurance, especially for repeated exposure.

descriptions.name: sodium sulfates
descriptions.description_en: Refined sulfate salts used in processing and acidity control. Health: Large sulfate doses can draw water into the intestine and cause diarrhea. Sodium-containing forms also add to total sodium intake.

descriptions.name: soja
descriptions.description_en: Soy in unspecified form, from whole beans to industrial isolates. Whole soy is nutritious, but most soy in processed food is heavily refined and frequently GM outside the EU.

descriptions.name: sorbate de potassium
descriptions.description_en: One of the most common mould inhibitors (E202), well tolerated and among the gentler preservatives. Some laboratory work suggests it may react with vitamin C, though food-level effects are not established.

descriptions.name: sorbitanes
descriptions.description_en: Sorbitan emulsifiers (E491–E495) used to stabilise fats in baked goods and confectionery. They belong to the synthetic emulsifier family under study for effects on the gut lining.

descriptions.name: sorbitol
descriptions.description_en: A polyol sweetener (E420) that is only partly absorbed, so it raises blood sugar less than sugar. EU law requires a laxative warning above 10%, as it commonly causes bloating and diarrhoea.

descriptions.name: soybean hemicellulose
descriptions.description_en: A processed fiber fraction extracted from soybeans and used to thicken, stabilize, or keep particles suspended. It is mainly an industrial texture ingredient. Health: Residual soy proteins may matter for people with a severe soy allergy, even though the additive itself is not considered highly toxic.

descriptions.name: spices
descriptions.description_en: Culinary herbs and spices such as basil, oregano and thyme. They are among the most antioxidant-dense foods by weight and replace salt as a source of flavour.

descriptions.name: spiruline
descriptions.description_en: A blue-green algae dense in plant protein, iron and B vitamins. Genuinely nutritious, though quality varies and it should be sourced from tested, contamination-free suppliers.

descriptions.name: stannous chloride
descriptions.description_en: A tin compound used mainly to preserve color in a limited number of canned foods. It requires strict concentration limits. Health: Excess inorganic tin can cause acute nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea. This is the principal established health concern.

descriptions.name: stearoyl lactylate de sodium
descriptions.description_en: Sodium stearoyl lactylate (E481), a dough conditioner that improves volume and shelf life in industrial bread. It is authorised at limited levels but never needed in traditionally made bread.

descriptions.name: stevia
descriptions.description_en: Steviol glycosides (E960) extracted from stevia leaves — plant-derived but heavily refined. Approved with a daily limit of 4 mg/kg, they add no calories, though the aftertaste means they are often blended with other sweeteners.

descriptions.name: stevia leaf
descriptions.description_en: Whole stevia leaf, dried or powdered, rather than the purified glycoside extract. It is the least processed form of stevia, with no calories and no blood sugar impact.

descriptions.name: substances laitieres modifiees
descriptions.description_en: A vague label covering dairy fractions altered or recombined industrially. It tells the consumer nothing about what is actually inside and signals a reconstituted rather than a real dairy product.

descriptions.name: sucralose
descriptions.description_en: A chlorinated artificial sweetener (E955) about 600 times sweeter than sugar. Approved by EFSA and the FDA, but studies suggest it may disturb gut bacteria, and it can form harmful compounds when heated in baking.

descriptions.name: sucre
descriptions.description_en: Refined sucrose, stripped of every nutrient. It is absorbed rapidly, driving blood-sugar spikes and insulin resistance, and regular intake contributes to obesity, type 2 diabetes and chronic inflammation.

descriptions.name: Sucre blanc raffiné
descriptions.description_en: Fully refined sucrose, stripped of all minerals. It is absorbed rapidly, spikes blood sugar and contributes to weight gain and metabolic disease when consumed regularly.

descriptions.name: sucre de canne
descriptions.description_en: Cane sugar, including raw, brown and demerara forms. It keeps a trace of molasses and minerals, but it is still around 95% sucrose and affects blood sugar much like white sugar.

descriptions.name: sucre de canne complet
descriptions.description_en: Unrefined whole cane sugar — rapadura, panela, muscovado, jaggery — and molasses. They keep the minerals refining strips out, but remain sugar and should be used sparingly.

descriptions.name: sucre de coco
descriptions.description_en: Coconut palm sugar, minimally refined and containing some minerals and inulin. Its glycemic index is slightly lower than white sugar, but it is still sugar.

descriptions.name: sucre de datte
descriptions.description_en: Whole dates ground into a powder, so the fibre and minerals stay in. It is the closest thing to sweetening with actual fruit, though still concentrated in sugar.

descriptions.name: sucre inverti
descriptions.description_en: Sugar split into glucose and fructose to boost sweetness and keep products moist. Metabolically it behaves like table sugar, with the same effect on blood sugar and weight.

descriptions.name: sucres
descriptions.description_en: A catch-all label covering the added refined sugars in a product. They deliver energy with no vitamins, minerals or fibre, and regular consumption is tied to metabolic disease.

descriptions.name: sucroglycerides
descriptions.description_en: Industrial emulsifiers produced by reacting sucrose with food fats. They help oil and water remain mixed and create a stable, smooth texture in highly formulated foods. Health: Some exposure scenarios may approach or exceed the group acceptable daily intake. Large amounts may also contribute to digestive discomfort.

descriptions.name: sulfate de cuivre
descriptions.description_en: Copper sulfate (E519), used as a processing aid and firming agent. Copper is essential in trace amounts but toxic in excess, causing liver and kidney damage, so food use is tightly capped.

descriptions.name: sulfite de calcium
descriptions.description_en: A sulfite preservative (E226) used mainly in processed vegetables and drinks. It is a declarable allergen above 10 mg/kg and best limited by anyone sensitive to sulfites.

descriptions.name: sulfite de potassium
descriptions.description_en: A sulfite preservative (E225) used to stop oxidation and spoilage. Safe for most people, but an EU-declarable allergen that can trigger breathing difficulties in asthmatics.

descriptions.name: sulfite de sodium
descriptions.description_en: A sulfite preservative (E221) that keeps foods pale and stops spoilage. It is an EU-declarable allergen above 10 mg/kg and can provoke breathing problems in people with asthma.

descriptions.name: sulfuric acid
descriptions.description_en: A strong industrial acid used in controlled food processing and pH adjustment. It is neutralized or diluted before the food is consumed. Health: Concentrated sulfuric acid is severely corrosive, but properly manufactured food should not retain that corrosive hazard.

descriptions.name: tahini
descriptions.description_en: Sesame paste and the traditional dips built on whole ingredients — hummus, baba ganoush, guacamole, tzatziki. Nutrient-dense and made from real foods.

descriptions.name: talc
descriptions.description_en: Food-grade talc is used to prevent sticking or clumping. Safety depends strongly on mineral purity, particle properties, and the absence of asbestos contamination. Health: Contaminated talc would be unacceptable and potentially harmful. Only material meeting strict food-grade purity standards should be used.

descriptions.name: tanin ferrique
descriptions.description_en: Iron tannate (E181), a colouring used on olives and some coatings. It is permitted at low levels but has little modern use and adds no nutritional value.

descriptions.name: tapioca dextrin
descriptions.description_en: A modified starch derived from cassava, used to coat, bulk and thicken. Like other dextrins, it is a refined carbohydrate that raises blood sugar quickly and adds no nutrients.

descriptions.name: tarama
descriptions.description_en: A spread made from salted fish roe. Traditional versions are simple, but industrial tarama is dominated by oil, salt and colouring, with a modest proportion of actual roe.

descriptions.name: tartaric acid esters of mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids
descriptions.description_en: Chemically modified fats used to strengthen dough, stabilize mixtures, and control texture. They are characteristic of industrial bakery and processed-food formulations. Health: No major specific disease risk is established at authorized levels. The relevant concern is cumulative intake and manufacturing impurities.

descriptions.name: tartrazine
descriptions.description_en: Yellow 5 (E102), a synthetic azo dye. EU law requires a warning that it may affect children's activity and attention; it can also trigger reactions in people sensitive to aspirin.

descriptions.name: taurine
descriptions.description_en: An amino acid the body produces naturally, added in large amounts to energy drinks. EFSA found no safety concern for taurine itself; the real issue is the caffeine and sugar it is usually paired with.

descriptions.name: tbhq
descriptions.description_en: Tert-butylhydroquinone (E319), a petroleum-derived antioxidant preservative. Not classified as a carcinogen by IARC, but high-dose animal studies show immune effects, and EFSA advises against use for infants.

descriptions.name: tea tree
descriptions.description_en: An essential oil with genuine antibacterial activity, used against acne. It must be diluted, as undiluted use causes irritation, and it is a recognised contact allergen that oxidises with age.

descriptions.name: tetraborate de sodium
descriptions.description_en: Borax (E285), permitted in the EU for caviar only. It is classified as toxic to reproduction under EU chemical law and banned from general food use in most countries, including the US.

descriptions.name: thaumatine
descriptions.description_en: A sweet protein (E957) extracted from the West African katemfe fruit, around 2,000 times sweeter than sugar. It is plant-derived and digested like any protein, but it is a concentrated industrial extract with a lingering liquorice aftertaste.

descriptions.name: the noir
descriptions.description_en: Black tea and rooibos. Black tea supplies theaflavins and moderate caffeine; rooibos is naturally caffeine-free and rich in antioxidants.

descriptions.name: the vert
descriptions.description_en: Green tea, rich in catechins including EGCG, with well-documented antioxidant activity. It provides gentle caffeine alongside L-theanine, which softens the stimulant effect.

descriptions.name: theine
descriptions.description_en: Theine is simply caffeine as found in tea, alongside theobromine from cocoa. Both are natural stimulants, gentler and longer-acting than coffee thanks to the tannins in tea.

descriptions.name: thon
descriptions.description_en: A nutritious source of protein and omega-3, but a large predator that accumulates methylmercury. Health agencies advise limiting intake, particularly for pregnant women and young children.

descriptions.name: tilapia
descriptions.description_en: A widely farmed white fish, affordable and lean but low in omega-3 and relatively high in omega-6. Farming conditions vary considerably, so sourcing matters.

descriptions.name: tobiko
descriptions.description_en: Flying fish roe used in sushi. It provides protein and omega-3, but it is very high in sodium and commercial versions are usually dyed and preserved.

descriptions.name: tofu
descriptions.description_en: Tofu, edamame and whole soybeans. Whole soy provides complete plant protein, calcium and isoflavones, and is far less processed than soy protein isolate.

descriptions.name: Toluène
descriptions.description_en: A solvent used in nail polish and adhesives. It is classified as toxic to reproduction in the EU, and its vapours affect the nervous system — good ventilation matters when using it.

descriptions.name: tomate
descriptions.description_en: Tomatoes in all forms, including paste and purée. Cooking actually increases the availability of lycopene, their signature antioxidant, making tomato paste a genuinely nutritious ingredient.

descriptions.name: triacetine
descriptions.description_en: A humectant and solvent (E1518) used to carry flavours and keep products moist. It breaks down into glycerol and acetic acid in the body and is considered safe at food levels.

descriptions.name: triclosan
descriptions.description_en: An antibacterial agent in some toothpastes, soaps and deodorants. The FDA banned it from consumer hand soaps in 2016; it is capped in the EU over hormonal effects and its contribution to antibiotic resistance.

descriptions.name: triethyl citrate
descriptions.description_en: A manufactured citrate ester used as a carrier, solvent, or plasticizer for flavors and coatings. Health: No major specific harm is established at authorized levels. Total exposure should remain within the acceptable daily intake.

descriptions.name: tripolyphosphate
descriptions.description_en: A phosphate (E451) used to make meat and seafood hold water, increasing their weight. It is permitted but contributes to a phosphate load that EFSA considers already high in European diets.

descriptions.name: vermicelles de blé
descriptions.description_en: Thin noodles made from refined wheat flour. Convenient and quick to cook, but a refined carbohydrate with little fibre unless made from whole grain.

descriptions.name: vert 3
descriptions.description_en: Fast Green FCF (E143), a synthetic dye that is not authorised as a food colour in the European Union. It remains permitted in the US, where the FDA is working to phase it out.

descriptions.name: viande rouge
descriptions.description_en: Plain red meat, rich in bioavailable iron, zinc and B12. Health bodies suggest capping intake at around 500 g cooked per week, and it is far preferable to processed meat.

descriptions.name: viande transformee
descriptions.description_en: Meat preserved by salting, curing, smoking or nitrites (bacon, ham, sausages, deli meats). Classified IARC Group 1 human carcinogen in 2015: regular intake raises colorectal cancer risk. Best kept occasional.

descriptions.name: vinaigre
descriptions.description_en: Vinegar, made by fermenting alcohol into acetic acid. Taken with a meal it modestly lowers the blood sugar response, and it flavours food without salt or sugar.

descriptions.name: vinaigre de riz
descriptions.description_en: Rice, sherry, malt and other traditional vinegars. All are simple fermented products used to add acidity and flavour without additives.

descriptions.name: vinaigre en poudre
descriptions.description_en: Vinegar dried onto a starch carrier, typically maltodextrin, to flavour crisps and seasoning mixes. It is a technical powder built for industrial dosing, not a natural vinegar.

descriptions.name: vitamine c
descriptions.description_en: Ascorbic acid (E300), used both as a nutrient and as a natural antioxidant to stop foods browning. It is essential for immunity, collagen and iron absorption.

descriptions.name: Vitamine E naturelle (tocophérol)
descriptions.description_en: Natural vitamin E (E306), used as an antioxidant to keep fats from going rancid. It protects both the food and the body's own cells.

descriptions.name: whey
descriptions.description_en: Whey, the liquid fraction of milk, rich in complete protein and branched-chain amino acids. A natural dairy component, though isolated protein powders are far more processed.

descriptions.name: xylitol
descriptions.description_en: A sugar alcohol used to replace sugar in chewing gum, candy, drinks, and low-sugar products. It is highly refined and can cause gas, abdominal cramps, bloating, or diarrhea when a large amount is consumed. Health: The main established concern is a dose-related laxative effect. People with irritable bowel syndrome or sensitivity to polyols may react at lower amounts.

descriptions.name: yaourt
descriptions.description_en: Plain yoghurt, milk fermented with live cultures. Fermentation makes it more digestible and adds beneficial bacteria — as long as no sugar has been added.

descriptions.name: zinc pyrithione
descriptions.description_en: An antifungal once common in anti-dandruff shampoos, banned in EU cosmetics since March 2022 after being classified toxic to reproduction. It remains permitted in some other markets.

descriptions.name: 청국장
descriptions.description_en: Cheonggukjang, a fast-fermented soybean paste rich in Bacillus subtilis and nattokinase. One of the most probiotic-dense traditional Korean foods.

descriptions.name: fécule de pomme de terre
descriptions.description_en: Starch extracted from potatoes by industrial washing and drying. It is gluten-free and thickens well, but it is a refined carbohydrate with a very high glycemic index and none of the tuber's fibre, potassium or vitamin C.

descriptions.name: farine de riz
descriptions.description_en: Milled white rice, naturally gluten-free and easy to digest. With the bran and germ removed it behaves like a fast sugar in the body, so wholegrain rice flour is the better option.

descriptions.name: protéine de blé
descriptions.description_en: Wheat gluten isolated by washing the starch out of the flour, then dried. It is protein-rich but low in lysine, and is used mainly to give industrial breads and meat substitutes their elasticity. Unsuitable in coeliac disease or gluten sensitivity.

descriptions.name: protéine de pois chiche
descriptions.description_en: Protein milled and water-separated from chickpeas. It supplies plant protein, fibre and iron with a milder taste than yellow pea protein, but it remains a fractioned ingredient rather than the whole pulse.

descriptions.name: farine de pois
descriptions.description_en: Dried yellow peas simply milled into flour, with no chemical extraction. Unlike a protein isolate it keeps the whole pea's fibre and starch, making it one of the least processed plant-protein ingredients.

descriptions.name: petit-lait en poudre
descriptions.description_en: Whey dried by high-temperature spray-drying, then used as a cheap source of protein, lactose and texture. It keeps most of whey's nutrients, but it is a dried, fractioned dairy ingredient and is high in lactose.

descriptions.name: brocoli
descriptions.description_en: Broccoli, a cruciferous vegetable rich in vitamin C, vitamin K and fibre, best known for the glucosinolates that release sulforaphane, studied for its protective role. Brief steaming preserves far more of these compounds than boiling.

descriptions.name: chou
descriptions.description_en: Cabbage, a very low-calorie cruciferous vegetable high in vitamin C, vitamin K and fibre. Raw it keeps the most vitamin C; fermented as sauerkraut or kimchi it also supplies lactic bacteria that support gut flora.

descriptions.name: farine de maïs
descriptions.description_en: Corn milled into flour or semolina. Unlike cornstarch it keeps part of the grain's protein and fibre, but its glycemic index stays high once cooked. Naturally gluten-free.

descriptions.name: oignon
descriptions.description_en: Onion, raw or dehydrated, a source of quercetin, sulphur compounds and prebiotic fructans that feed gut bacteria. Dehydrated onion keeps part of these antioxidants and seasons food without adding salt.

descriptions.name: algue
descriptions.description_en: Edible seaweed, one of the few plant sources of iodine, alongside soluble fibre, iron and magnesium. Nutritionally valuable, though its high iodine and sodium content makes large daily amounts inadvisable.

descriptions.name: fruit du moine
descriptions.description_en: A sweetener from luo han guo, a small Asian melon whose mogrosides are 150–200 times sweeter than sugar with no calories and no effect on blood sugar. Well tolerated, though it is a concentrated extract, often blended with erythritol.
